Because of tip, guṇa for the penultimate of the root. By अभ्यस्तानामादिः (*abhyastānāmādiḥ*) (Pā. Sū. 6-1-189) the anudātta accent comes *[as supplied: "ಅಮೃದಾತ್ತಸ್ವರ", i.e. a misprint for the anudātta accent]*.

मिथुनासः (*mithunāsaḥ*)—mitha is a Saura root. By क्षुधिपिशिमिथिभ्यः कित् (*kṣudhipiśimithibhyaḥ kit*) (Uṇ. Sū. 3-335) the suffix unan. By vyatyaya (interchange) it has the final accent. When jas follows, by आज्जसेरसुक् (*ājjaserasuk*) (Pā. Sū. 7-1-50) the augment asuk is added to it.

तस्थुः (*tasthuḥ*)—the root ष्ठा गतिनिवृत्तौ (*ṣṭhā gatinivṛttau*). By छंदसिलुज् लज् लिटः (*chaṃdasiluj laj liṭaḥ*) the liṭ in the present sense. A form ending in the third person plural. The tiṅanta nighāta accent comes. || 11 ||

#### Ṛk 12
**॥ संहितापाठः ॥**
> पंच॑पादं पि॒तरं॒ द्वाद॑शाकृतिं दि॒व आ॑हुः॒ परे॒ अर्धे॑ पुरी॒षिणं॑ ।
> अथे॒मे अ॒न्य उप॑रे विचक्ष॒णं स॒प्तच॑क्रे॒ षळ॑र आहु॒रर्पि॑तं ॥
> ॥ १२ ॥

*[ದವಹಾರಃ]* *(garbled label as supplied; repaired by the script to Pada-pāṭha)*

**॥ पदपाठः ॥**
> पंचपादं । पितरं । द्वादशआकृतिं । दिवः । आहुः । परे । अर्धे । पुरीषिणं ।
> अथ । इमे । अन्ये । उपरे ! विचक्षणं । सप्तचक्रे । षट्सअरे । आहुः । अर्पितं ॥
> ॥ १२ ॥

**॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥**
> पंचपादं पंचसंख्याकर्त्वात्मकपादोपेतं । एतद्देमंतशिशिरयोरेकत्वाभिप्रायं । पितरं सर्वस्य प्रीणयितारं द्वादशाकृतिं द्वादशमासा एवाकृतयो
> यस्य तादृशं पुरीषिणं वृष्टुदकेन तद्वंतं प्रीणयितारं वा । पुरीषमित्युदकनाम । उक्तलक्षणं संवत्सरचक्रं दिवो द्युलोकस्य परेऽर्धे । तात्स्थात्ताच्छब्दं ।
> परस्मिन्नर्धे०तरिक्षलक्षणेवस्थित आदित्य इत्यर्थः । तस्मिन्नर्पितमाहुः । एतदुत्तरत्र
> स्थितमत्राप्यनुषज्यते । यद्यत्रार्पितं तत्तदधीनं अतः संवत्सरं सूर्यायत्तमाहुरित्यर्थः । अथेमेपि चान्ये केचन वेदवादिन एवमाहुः । किमिति । उपरे ।
> उपरमंतेऽस्मिन् उपरताः प्राणिनोऽत्रेति वोपरः संवत्सरः । तस्मिन्निदृशे । सप्त-

### Printed p. 360
*Running head: 360 Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā [ಮಂ. ೧. ಅ. ೨೨. ಸೂ. ೧೬೪] (as supplied).*

[Continuing the Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya of Ṛk 12, from the word "sapta-" cut off at the foot of the previous page:]
> चक्रे । सप्तादित्यरश्मयस्तद्वारेण चक्रस्थानीया यस्य स तथोक्तः । यद्वा । आयनर्तुमासपक्षाहोरात्रिमुहूर्तानि सप्त सप्त चक्राणि पुनः पुनः क्रममाणानि यस्य
> तादृशे । षळरे षडृतव एवारा नाभौ प्रत्युताः संबद्धा यस्य तथोक्तलक्षणे
> संवत्सरे रथे विचक्षणं विविधदर्शनकरमादित्यमर्पितमाहुः । एतदुक्तं भवति ।
> अमुमादित्यं दक्षिणोत्तररूपभिन्नगतेस्तीव्रमंदादिभावस्य च कालाधीनत्वात्तदधीनमाहुः । अन्ये तु संवत्सराद्यात्मकस्य कालस्य सूर्यगमनागमनसाध्यत्वात्तदायत्तत्वमाहुरिति ॥

**प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)**
पंचपादं (*paṃcapādaṃ*)—him who has five feet in the form of seasons; पितरं (*pitaraṃ*)—the giver of delight, or him who is of the nature of a father; द्वादशाकृतिं (*dvādaśākṛtiṃ*)—him who has the twelve months as his limbs; पुरीषिणं (*purīṣiṇaṃ*)—him who is filled with rain-water: the Āditya; दिवः (*divaḥ*)—of the heaven-world; हरे अर्धे (*hare ardhe*) *[as supplied: हरे (*hare*); the Saṃhitā word is परे (*pare*)]*—in the highest place (as one placed there); आहुः (*āhuḥ*)—(some knowers of the truth) say; अथ इमे अन्वे (*atha ime anve*) *[as supplied: अन्वे (*anve*); the Saṃhitā word is अन्ये (*anye*)]*—and these others, some more of the Vedavādins; सप्तचक्रे (*saptacakre*)—in that which consists of seven parts such as the ayanas; षळरे (*ṣaḷare*)—having six spokes in the form of seasons; उपरे (*upare*)—in time in the form of the year; विचक्षणं (*vicakṣaṇaṃ*)—the Āditya, who is the cause of varied sights; अर्पितं (*arpitaṃ*)—as one placed *[as supplied: आर्पिसल्पट्टिरुवनन्नागि (*ārpisalpaṭṭiruvanannāgi*)]*; आहुः (*āhuḥ*)—they say.

**भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)**
Some knowers of the truth say that the Āditya, who has five feet in the form of seasons, who is of the nature of a father, who has the forms of the twelve months, and who is filled with rain-water, is placed in the highest position of the heaven-world. Other Vedavādins say that the Āditya, the cause of varied sights, is placed (established) in time in the form of the year, which consists of seven parts such as the ayanas and has six spokes in the form of seasons.

**Printed English**
They have termed the five-footed, twelve-formed parent, Purishin, when in the further hemisphere of the sky: and others have termed him Arpita, when in the hither (portion of the sky); shining in his seven-wheeled (car), each (wheel) having six spokes.

**विशेषविषयगळु (Viśeṣaviṣayagaḷu)**
Sāyaṇa has stated the total purport of this Ṛk in this way: अमुमादित्यं दक्षिणोत्तररूपभिन्नगतेः तीव्रमंदादिभावस्य च कालाधीनत्वात्तदधीन (*amumādityaṃ dakṣiṇottararūpabhinnagateḥ tīvramaṃdādibhāvasya ca kālādhīnatvāttadadhīna*) (continued on the next page)

### Printed p. 361
*Running head: Ṛgveda-saṃhitā 361 [ಅ ೨. ಅ. ೩. ವ. ೧೬ ] (as supplied).*

माहुः (*māhuḥ*). अन्ये तु संवत्सराद्यात्मकस्य कालस्य सूर्यगमनागमनसाध्यत्वात् तदायत्तत्वमाहुः (*anye tu saṃvatsarādyātmakasya kālasya sūryagamanāgamanasādhyatvāt tadāyattatvamāhuḥ*) *ಇತಿ*. One opinion is that the courses of the Āditya, in the form of the southern and northern solstices, and likewise his intensity or mildness, are subject to time in the form of the year, and that therefore the Āditya is subject to time. Another opinion is that, since time in the form of the year depends on the going and coming of the sun, time in the form of the year depends on the sun. In the present Ṛk the Āditya in the form of the year is described.

पंचपादं (*paṃcapādaṃ*)—पंचसंख्याकऋत्वात्मकपादोपेतं एतत् हेमंत शिशिरयोः एकत्वाभिप्रायं (*paṃcasaṃkhyākaṛtvātmakapādopetaṃ etat hemaṃta śiśirayoḥ ekatvābhiprāyaṃ*). Since the Hemanta season and the Śiśira season have the same quality, if both are reckoned as one season, then only five seasons are the parts of the year. Here "five-footed" is an epithet of the year. This mantra is recited also in the Praśna Upaniṣad. There Śaṅkarācārya explains this word as: पंचर्तवः पादा इवास्य संवत्सरात्मन आदित्यस्य । तैरस्सा पाद्यरिवर्तुभिरावर्तते । हेमंतशिशिरावेकीकृत्येयं कल्पना (*paṃcartavaḥ pādā ivāsya saṃvatsarātmana ādityasya | tairassā pādyarivartubhirāvartate | hemaṃtaśiśirāvekīkṛtyeyaṃ kalpanā*), that is, the five seasons that are like feet of the Āditya who is of the nature of the year. (Pra. U. 1-11.)

द्वादशाकृतिं (*dvādaśākṛtiṃ*)—द्वादश मासा एव आकृतयो यस्य तादृशं (*dvādaśa māsā eva ākṛtayo yasya tādṛśaṃ*); that is, the Āditya of the nature of the year, whose limbs are the twelve months. The form of the Āditya furnished with all these seventeen limbs is described in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa:

तस्य सप्तदश सामिधेन्यः । सप्तदशो वै संवत्सरो द्वादशमासाः पंचर्तवः संवत्सरः प्रजापतिः (*tasya saptadaśa sāmidhenyaḥ | saptadaśo vai saṃvatsaro dvādaśamāsāḥ paṃcartavaḥ saṃvatsaraḥ prajāpatiḥ*)
(Śa. Brā. 6-2-2-8)

Prajāpati is the year, having seventeen limbs, with twelve months and five seasons; thus the relation between the sāmidhenī mantras, which are a part of the sacrifice, and Prajāpati is shown. The purport is that, since the limbs of the year are seventeen, these mantras also must be seventeen in number.

पितरं (*pitaraṃ*)—सर्वस्य प्रीणयितारं (*sarvasya prīṇayitāraṃ*), "one who gives delight to all": this is an epithet of the wheel of the year; that is, since the identity of the wheel of the year and the Āditya is stated here, it must be understood that the word पितरं (*pitaraṃ*) is an epithet of the Āditya also. If it is an epithet of the Āditya, it would not be wrong to give the established meaning "father". Why? Because:

पिता नोऽसि पिता नो बोधीति । एष वै पिता य एष तपत्येष उ प्रवर्ग्यस्तदेतमेवैतत्प्रीणाति तस्मादाह पिता नोऽसि पिता नो बोधीति नमस्तेऽस्तु। (*pitā no 'si pitā no bodhīti | eṣa vai pitā ya eṣa tapatyeṣa u pravargyastadetamevaitatprīṇāti tasmādāha pitā no 'si pitā no bodhīti namaste 'stu|*)
(Śa. Brā. 14-1-4-15)

### Printed p. 362
*Running head: 362 ರಾಯಣಭಾವ್ಯಸಹಿತಾ [ಮಂ. ೧. ಅ. ೨೨ ಸೂ. ೧೬೪ (as supplied, garbled; the intended running head is Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā).*

The Āditya who shines in the atmosphere is the father of us all; he is the giver of delight and the cause of contentment to us all; he is of the form of the pravargya. Since he is addressed thus, here also he may be called father. Both these meanings are contained in the word. This meaning can be given with reference to the year also. Why? Because:

अथो प्रजननमेतत्संवत्सरो वा ऋतव्याः संवत्सरः प्रजननं प्रजननमेवैतदुपदधाति (*atho prajananametatsaṃvatsaro vā ṛtavyāḥ saṃvatsaraḥ prajananaṃ prajananamevaitadupadadhāti*)
(Śa. Brā. 8-7-1-1) *[as supplied: "ಶ ಬ್ರಾ."]*

In such sentences, since it is said that the power of generation is itself in the form of the year, and that all beings were produced from the year, the established meaning "father" can be given. Sāyaṇa has given only the meaning प्रीणयितारं (*prīṇayitāraṃ*), "giving contentment". In his commentary on the Praśna Upaniṣad, Śaṅkarācārya explains this word thus: सर्वस्य जनयित्कृत्वात्पितृत्वं तस्य (*sarvasya janayitkṛtvātpitṛtvaṃ tasya*) (संवत्सरात्मन आदित्यस्य (*saṃvatsarātmana ādityasya*)); that is, because the Āditya of the nature of the year is the progenitor of all, he has fatherhood. (Pra. U. 1-11.)

पुरीषिणं (*purīṣiṇaṃ*)—पुरीषमित्युदकनाम (*purīṣamityudakanāma*): this word is read among the names of water. सर्व (*sarva*) कामानां पूरकं उदकं (*kāmānāṃ pūrakaṃ udakaṃ*): the meaning is "by water which fulfils all desired objects". When stating the precise etymology of this word, the author of the Nirukta, quoting the Ṛk

देवानां माने प्रथमा अतिष्ठन् कृंतत्रादेषामुसरा उदायन् । त्रयस्तपंति पृथिवीमनूपा द्वा बृबूकं वहतः पुरीषं (*devānāṃ māne prathamā atiṣṭhan kṛṃtatrādeṣāmusarā udāyan | trayastapaṃti pṛthivīmanūpā dvā bṛbūkaṃ vahataḥ purīṣaṃ*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-27-23)

shows there, with पुरीषं प्रीणातेः पूरयतेर्वा (*purīṣaṃ prīṇāteḥ pūrayatervā*), that this word is formed from a root प्प (*ppa*) *[sic: as supplied]* meaning "fill" or "satisfy". (सि (*si*)- 2-22 *[as supplied: the abbreviation is odd; reported]*.) The epithet "purīṣī" is well known for the Āditya, since he possesses water which fills the world or gives satisfaction to the world, or since he is pervaded by water. Even though water is not contained within the Āditya, this epithet is applied because the Āditya revolves in the midst of water or because he is the producer of water; this is understood from many sentences of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa:

अपां गंभन्तीदेति । एतद्वापां गंभिष्टं यत्रैष एतत्तपति (*apāṃ gaṃbhantīdeti | etadvāpāṃ gaṃbhiṣṭaṃ yatraiṣa etattapati*)
(Śa. Brā. 7-5-1-8) *[as supplied: "ಶ ಬ್ರಾ."]*

In the atmosphere, in the midst of deep water, the Āditya shines.

### Printed p. 363
*Running head: Ṛgveda-saṃhitā 363 [ಅ. ೨. ಅ. ೩. ಪ. ೧೬] (as supplied: "ಪ." for "ವ.").*

अग्ने दिवोर्णमच्छा जिगासीति । अपो वा अस्य दिवोर्णस्ता .... .... .... या रोचने परस्तात्सूर्यस्य याश्चावस्तादुपतिष्ठंत अप इति रोचनो ह नामैष लोको यत्रैष एतत्तपति तद्याश्चैतं परेणापो याश्चावरेण ता एतदाह (*agne divorṇamacchā jigāsīti | apo vā asya divorṇastā .... .... .... yā rocane parastātsūryasya yāścāvastādupatiṣṭhaṃta apa iti rocano ha nāmaiṣa loko yatraiṣa etattapati tadyāścaitaṃ pareṇāpo yāścāvareṇa tā etadāha*)
(Śa. Brā. 7-1-1-24) *[the dotted gaps are in the print]*

O Agni, in the heaven-world all thy brilliance shines in the form of the Āditya. Thou shinest in the stream that is in the atmosphere. That stream is pervaded by the water of the atmosphere. That stream of water has overspread (*as supplied: "ಮಾರಿಹೋಗಿದೆ"*) even the orb of brilliance of the Āditya. In the midst of the stream spreading below, above and all round, the Agni in the form of the Āditya is shining; thus it is described. Further:

सर्वाणि ह त्वेव भूतानि । सर्वे देवा एषोऽग्निश्चित अपो वै सर्वे देवा सर्वाणि भूतानि ता हैता आप एवैषोऽग्निश्चितस्तस्य नाव्या एव परिश्रितस्ताः षष्टिश्च त्रीणि च शतानि भवंति षष्टिश्च ह वै त्रीणि च शतान्यादित्यं नाव्या अभिरक्षंत्यथ यदंतरा नाव्ये तत्सूददोहा (*sarvāṇi ha tveva bhūtāni | sarve devā eṣo 'gniścita apo vai sarve devā sarvāṇi bhūtāni tā haitā āpa evaiṣo 'gniścitastasya nāvyā eva pariśritastāḥ ṣaṣṭiśca trīṇi ca śatāni bhavaṃti ṣaṣṭiśca ha vai trīṇi ca śatānyādityaṃ nāvyā abhirakṣaṃtyatha yadaṃtarā nāvye tatsūdadohā*)
(Śa. Brā. 10-5-4-14)

Here, speaking of the likeness between the fire-altar and the orb of the Āditya, it is stated that the sacrificial fire is itself all beings and all deities, that all beings are the all-pervading water, and the three hundred and sixty streams that surround the orb of the Āditya are described as equal to the three hundred and sixty bricks on the circumference of the fire-altar. It is explained that these streams flow enveloping the sun and facing him. Sāyaṇa explains that, because the sun's rays are the cause of the streams of water, the rays themselves are spoken of figuratively as streams, saying अर्चिसो ह्यापसूरकिरणानामेव वृष्टिकर्तृकत्वात् कार्यकारणयोरभेदेन अर्चिर्वा अप इत्युक्तं (*arciso hyāpasūrakiraṇānāmeva vṛṣṭikartṛkatvāt kāryakāraṇayorabhedena arcirvā apa ityuktaṃ*). Thus, because he is surrounded by water and, through his rays, is the cause of the flow of water, the epithet "purīṣa" explains the nature of the Āditya.

Sāyaṇa first explains उदकवंतं (*udakavaṃtaṃ*), and then gives a second meaning also, प्रीणयितारं वा (*prīṇayitāraṃ vā*), "giving delight to beings". As both meanings are possible according to the etymology of the author of the Nirukta quoted above, and since all life in the world is full of delight through the Āditya alone, either meaning may be given here.

उपरे (*upare*)—उपरमंते अस्मिन् उपरताः प्राणिनः अत्र इति वा उपरः संवत्सरः (*uparamaṃte asmin uparatāḥ prāṇinaḥ atra iti vā uparaḥ saṃvatsaraḥ*). Living beings come to rest here, that is, they attain death, without motion; since the word means this

### Printed p. 364
*Running head: 364 Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā [ ಮಂ. ೧ ಅ. ೨೨. ಸೂ. ೧೬೪] (as supplied).*

Sāyaṇa explains that "upara" means the year. For उपरमंते (*uparamaṃte*) in this sense there is also room to explain it as उपगम्य रमंते (*upagamya ramaṃte*), "approach and rejoice". Thus: the author of the Nirukta, showing the etymology of the word "upara" (Ni. 2-21; here it is a synonym of cloud), gives two explanations: उप रमंतेऽस्मिन्नभ्राणि (*upa ramaṃte 'sminnabhrāṇi*) and उप रता आप इति वा (*upa ratā āpa iti vā*). Durgācārya, commenting on this, says उपगम्य रमंते अस्मिन्नभ्राणि (*upagamya ramaṃte asminnabhrāṇi*): here the clouds gather together and show their joy. In the same way, in the present Ṛk also, उपरमंते (*uparamaṃte*) may be explained as "they experience the happiness obtained through plenty of food", and उपरताः (*uparatāḥ*) as "they are at rest", that is, "they attain a state without motion (they get death)". The year causes plenty of food and is the cause of contentment; and likewise, as the years, filled with days and nights, pass away, it is the cause of the death of living beings also. There are Śruti sentences showing both these views:

त्रीणि वा इमानि पंचविधानि । संवत्सरोऽग्निः पुरुषस्तेषां पंचविधा अन्नं पानग्ग् श्रीज्योतिरमृतं यदेव संवत्सरेऽन्नं तदन्नं या आपस्तत्पानग्ग् रात्रिरेव श्रीः श्रियाग्ग् हैतद्रात्र्याग्ग् सर्वाणि भूतानि संवसंत्यहर्ज्योतिरादित्योऽमृतमित्यधिदेवतं (*trīṇi vā imāni paṃcavidhāni | saṃvatsaro 'gniḥ puruṣasteṣāṃ paṃcavidhā annaṃ pānagg śrījyotiramṛtaṃ yadeva saṃvatsare 'nnaṃ tadannaṃ yā āpastatpānagg rātrireva śrīḥ śriyāgg haitadrātryāgg sarvāṇi bhūtāni saṃvasaṃtyaharjyotirādityo 'mṛtamityadhidevataṃ*)
(Śa. Brā. 10-2-6-16)

There are three things that have fivefold wealth: the year, Agni and the Puruṣa. Food, drink, prosperity (happiness), brilliance and immortality are their five transformations. As much food as there is in the year, so much is its nourishment; as much as there is water, so much is the drink; since all beings find happiness in the night alone, the night is happiness; the day is brilliance and the Āditya is immortality. Thus praising the abundance of wealth of the year, it goes on:

सोऽयं संवत्सरः प्रजापतिः .... .... .... .... तस्मादाहुस्संवत्सरः सर्वे कामा इति न ह संवत्सरात्कश्चन बहिर्धा कामोऽस्ति (*so 'yaṃ saṃvatsaraḥ prajāpatiḥ .... .... .... .... tasmādāhussaṃvatsaraḥ sarve kāmā iti na ha saṃvatsarātkaścana bahirdhā kāmo 'sti*)
(*as supplied:* "ಪ. ಬ್ರಾ. 10-2-4-1"; the dotted gaps are in the print)

Prajāpati is the year, and Agni is the reflection of every kind of desired object. The year in the form of Prajāpati, wishing to fulfil its desires, strove and itself filled itself with all kinds of desired objects. Therefore the year, the reflection of Prajāpati, was filled with desired objects. Thus the nature of the year is praised: there is no desired object outside the year. Since the year is also the support of every kind of desired object, the meaning संवत्सरे उपरमंते प्राणिनः (*saṃvatsare uparamaṃte prāṇinaḥ*), "living beings rejoice in the year", can be given. Secondly:

### Printed p. 365
*Running head: Ṛgveda-saṃhitā 365 [ಅ. ೨. ಅ. ೩. ವ. ೧೬ ] (as supplied).*

एष वै मृत्युर्यत्संवत्सरः । एष हि मर्त्यानामहोरात्राभ्यामायुः क्षिणोत्यथ म्रियंते तस्मादेष एव मत्युः स यो हैतं मृत्युग्ं संवत्सरं वेद न हास्यैष पुरा जरसोऽहोरात्राभ्यामायु: क्षिणोति सर्वग्ंहैवायुरेति (*eṣa vai mṛtyuryatsaṃvatsaraḥ | eṣa hi martyānāmahorātrābhyāmāyuḥ kṣiṇotyatha mriyaṃte tasmādeṣa eva matyuḥ sa yo haitaṃ mṛtyugṃ saṃvatsaraṃ veda na hāsyaiṣa purā jaraso 'horātrābhyāmāyu: kṣiṇoti sarvagṃhaivāyureti*)
(Śa. Brā. 10-4-3-1)

The year is like death. Prajāpati, in the form of time, destroys the world of mortals through the days and nights. Therefore the year is like the Ender. He who knows this attains the full span of his life; otherwise untimely death befalls him. For such:

एष उ एवांतकः । एष हि मर्त्यानामायुषोऽन्तं गच्छति। (*eṣa u evāṃtakaḥ | eṣa hi martyānāmāyuṣo 'ntaṃ gacchati|*)
(Śa. Brā. 10-4-3-2)

The year is the Ender. Prajāpati, in the form of time, is the ender of the lives of all beings through the days and nights. Since this is said, the second meaning given by Sāyaṇa, उपरताः प्राणिन अत्र इति वा उपरः संवत्सरः (*uparatāḥ prāṇina atra iti vā uparaḥ saṃvatsaraḥ*), is fitting.

सप्तचक्रे (*saptacakre*)—सप्त आदित्यरश्मयस्तद्वारेण चक्रस्थानीया यस्य स तथोक्तः। (*sapta ādityaraśmayastadvāreṇa cakrasthānīyā yasya sa tathoktaḥ|*) That is, with reference to the Āditya, "he who has the seven rays of the Āditya in the place of wheels"; and यद्वा । आयनर्तुमासपक्षा होरात्रमुहूर्तानि सप्त सप्त चक्राणि पुनःपुनः क्रममाणानि यस्य तादृशे संवत्सररूपे रथे (*yadvā | āyanartumāsapakṣā horātramuhūrtāni sapta sapta cakrāṇi punaḥpunaḥ kramamāṇāni yasya tādṛśe saṃvatsararūpe rathe*). Or: the ayana, season, month, fortnight, day, night and muhūrta are the seven parts. Thus with reference to the year it is explained as: in the chariot in the form of the year, which, furnished with such parts, revolves again and again like a wheel.

It may be said that in this Ṛk, by the above descriptions, the nature of the Āditya, who is beyond time and abides above the highest heaven-world, is explained from one point of view, and, secondly, the movements of the Āditya, who is subject to time, from another point of view. If, further, it is said that, as described in some earlier Ṛks, the Ṛk is explained from yet another point of view and praises also the Āditya who is of the nature of the Supreme Self, then a still more extended meaning must be given to the word सप्तचक्रे (*saptacakre*).

अथ वा एकशतविधः । सप्तविधमभिसंपद्यत एकशतधा वासावादित्यो विहितः सप्तसु देवलोकेषु प्रतिष्ठितः सप्त वै देवलोकाश्चतस्रो दिशस्त्रय इमे लोका एते वै सप्त देवलोकास्तेष्टेव प्रतिष्ठितः (*atha vā ekaśatavidhaḥ | saptavidhamabhisaṃpadyata ekaśatadhā vāsāvādityo vihitaḥ saptasu devalokeṣu pratiṣṭhitaḥ sapta vai devalokāścatasro diśastraya ime lokā ete vai sapta devalokāsteṣṭeva pratiṣṭhitaḥ*)
(Śa. Brā. 10-2-4-4) *[as supplied: "ಶ. ಬ್ರಾ, ೧೦-೨-೪-೪"]*

### Printed p. 366
*Running head: 366 ಸಾಯುಧಭಾಷ್ಯಸಹಿತಾ [ ಮಂ. ೧. ಆ. ೨೨. ಸೂ.೧೬೪] (as supplied, garbled; the intended running head is Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā).*

The Āditya, who is of the form of Agni, is of a hundred-and-one-fold nature (101): his rays are a hundredfold, and if his own form is added it becomes a hundred-and-one-fold. But this hundred-and-one-fold nature may also be summed up as sevenfold. The Āditya is established in this sevenfold universe. The four directions and the three worlds beginning with the earth together make the seven kinds of divine worlds. In these seven worlds the Āditya is established.

यद्वैकशतविधः । सप्तविधमभिसंपद्यत एकशतधा वा असावादित्यो विहित सप्तस्वतुषु सप्तषु स्तोमेषु सप्तसु पृष्ठेषु सप्तसु च्छंदस्सु सप्तसु प्राणेषु सप्तसु दिक्षु प्रतिष्ठितः (*yadvaikaśatavidhaḥ | saptavidhamabhisaṃpadyata ekaśatadhā vā asāvādityo vihita saptasvatuṣu saptaṣu stomeṣu saptasu pṛṣṭheṣu saptasu cchaṃdassu saptasu prāṇeṣu saptasu dikṣu pratiṣṭhitaḥ*)
(Śa. Brā. 10-2-4-5)

This Āditya, of a hundred-and-one-fold nature, is established in the universe as sevenfold: in the seven seasons *[the Kannada adds in brackets: it has been explained before which the seven seasons are]*, the seven stomas, the seven pṛṣṭhas (sāmans), the seven metres, the seven breaths and the seven directions.

यद्वैैकशतविधः । सप्तविधमभिसंपद्यत एकशतधा वा असावादित्यो विहितः सप्ताक्षरे ब्रह्मन् प्रतिष्ठितः सप्ताक्षरं वै बह्मर्गित्येकमक्षरं यजुरिति द्वे सामेति द्वेऽथ यदतोऽन्यद्ब्रह्मैव तद्दव्यक्षरं वै ब्रह्म तदेतत्सर्व सप्ताक्षरं ब्रह्म तस्मिन्नेष प्रतिष्ठितः (*yadvaiaikaśatavidhaḥ | saptavidhamabhisaṃpadyata ekaśatadhā vā asāvādityo vihitaḥ saptākṣare brahman pratiṣṭhitaḥ saptākṣaraṃ vai bahmargityekamakṣaraṃ yajuriti dve sāmeti dve 'tha yadato 'nyadbrahmaiva taddavyakṣaraṃ vai brahma tadetatsarva saptākṣaraṃ brahma tasminneṣa pratiṣṭhitaḥ*)
(Śa. Brā. "10-24-6" *as supplied*; the first word is printed with a doubled sign, kept)

The Āditya, of a hundred-and-one-fold nature, is established in Brahman, who has seven syllables. Brahman is of the nature of seven syllables: that of the form of the Ṛk is one, that of the form of the Yajus is two, the Sāman is two, and that of the nature of Brahman itself is two; altogether Brahman, whose nature is of seven syllables, is the universe. In this all-pervading Brahman the Āditya is established. Thus the various forms of the sevenfold Āditya are described. If the substance of the fourth brāhmaṇa of this chapter of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, quoted here, is gathered together:

संवत्सरो वै प्रजापतिः । अग्निरु सर्वॆ कामाः सोऽयं संवत्सरः । .... .... .. स यः स संवत्सरोऽसौ स आदित्यः .... .... .... (स) सप्तविधमभिसंपद्यते । .... .... .... सप्तविधो ना अग्रे प्रजापतिरसृज्यत (*saṃvatsaro vai prajāpatiḥ | agniru sarvè kāmāḥ so 'yaṃ saṃvatsaraḥ | .... .... .. sa yaḥ sa saṃvatsaro 'sau sa ādityaḥ .... .... .... (sa) saptavidhamabhisaṃpadyate | .... .... .... saptavidho nā agre prajāpatirasṛjyata*)
(Śa. Brā. 10-2-4) *[the print gives this reference twice, once as "ಶ. ಬಾ.. ೧೦-೨-೪" and once as "ಶ. ಬ್ರಾ. ೧೦-೨-೪"; the dotted gaps are in the print]*

The year is Prajāpati; Agni is the year; the year is the Āditya. Since Prajāpati was created in the beginning as sevenfold, it may be said that the point that the Āditya, who is of the nature of the year, is also established in the seven (seasons and the rest) and is all-pervading, is indicated by सप्तचक्रे अर्पितं आहुः (*saptacakre arpitaṃ āhuḥ*).

विचक्षणं (*vicakṣaṇaṃ*)—विविधदर्शनकरमादित्यं (*vividhadarśanakaramādityaṃ*). It is explained as: he who looks upon the world in different ways, through his different forms. The author of the Nirukta has explained it as विचक्षतेऽभिविसश्यंति (*vicakṣate 'bhivisaśyaṃti*) (Ni. 12-27). The author of the Nirukta

quoting the Ṛk

त्रयः केशिन ऋतुथा वि चक्षते संवत्सरे वपत एक एषां । विश्वमेको अभि चष्टे शचीभिध्र्राजिरेकस्य ददृशे न रूपं (*trayaḥ keśina ṛtuthā vi cakṣate saṃvatsare vapata eka eṣāṃ | viśvameko abhi caṣṭe śacībhidhrrājirekasya dadṛśe na rūpaṃ*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-164-49)

explains that Agni in the terrestrial form, the Āditya abiding in the heaven-world, and Vāyu abiding in the atmosphere, shining at their respective times of the year, regard the world with a benevolent mind. In the same sense the word विचक्षणं (*vicakṣaṇaṃ*) is used in the present Ṛk too. This word also has the meaning "learned", so that the nature of the Āditya can be stated as "wise, all-knowing".

वैश्वानर तव धामान्या चके येभिः स्वर्विदभवो विचक्षण (*vaiśvānara tava dhāmānyā cake yebhiḥ svarvidabhavo vicakṣaṇa*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-3-10)

प्र ते बभ्रू विचक्षण शंसामि गोषणो नपात् (*pra te babhrū vicakṣaṇa śaṃsāmi goṣaṇo napāt*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 4-32-22)

As in these and other Ṛks the meaning "wise" results, so in the present Ṛk also it may be understood as the all-knowing Āditya. On the whole, the divine nature of the Āditya, who holds in his control the time that governs the world and is the lord of the three worlds, and another nature of his, which manifests its movements joined with time and is subject to time and worldly, are both described together in this Ṛk.

*Grammar (transcribed, not explained):*
पंच पादम् (*paṃca pādam*)—पंच पादाः यस्य तम् (*paṃca pādāḥ yasya tam*). In a bahuvrīhi the accent of the first member comes.
अहुः (*ahuḥ*)—the root ब्रूञ् व्यक्तायां वाचि (*brūñ vyaktāyāṃ vāci*). When the laṭ third person plural follows, by ब्रुवः पंचानामादित आहो ब्रुवः (*bruvaḥ paṃcānāmādita āho bruvaḥ*) (Pā. Sū. 3-4-48 *as supplied*) the substitute āha for the root; the substitute us for the ending. Because it follows a non-verb, the nighāta accent comes.
पुरीषिणम् (*purīṣiṇam*)—पुरीषमस्य अस्ति इति पुरीषिणम् (*purīṣamasya asti iti purīṣiṇam*). By अत इनि ठनौ (*ata ini ṭhanau*) (Pā. Sū. 5-2-115) the suffix ini in the possessive sense. By the accent of the suffix it has the final accent. A form ending in the accusative singular.
विचक्षणम् (*vicakṣaṇam*)—the root चक्षिज् व्यक्तायां वाचि (*cakṣij vyaktāyāṃ vāci*). The i becomes anudātta and gets the designation it. Because it is anudātta-it, by अनुदात्तेतश्च हलादेः (*anudāttetaśca halādeḥ*) (Pā. Sū. 3-2-149) the suffix yuc. By युवोरनाकौ (*yuvoranākau*) (Pā. Sū. 7-1-1) ana is the substitute for it. By चितः (*citaḥ*)- (Pā. Sū. 6-1-163) the final accent comes. In a prādi compound the accent of the kṛdutarapada comes. *(The window ends here, as supplied.)*

**॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥**
*[ಸಯಣಭಾಷ್ಯಂ]* *(garbled label as supplied; repaired by the script)*
> पंचारे पंचर्तुरूपैररैर्युक्ते चक्रे संवत्सरात्मके परिवर्तमाने संवत्सरपरिवत्सरादिरूपेण पुनःपुनरावर्तमाने सति तस्मिन्कालचक्रे विश्वा भुवनानि सर्वाणि

> नास्तित्यर्थः ॥

*Gist:* While the five-spoked wheel of the year turns, all worlds rest in it; its heavily loaded axle is not strained and its nave does not wear out.

**प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)**
पंचारे (*paṃcāre*)—furnished with five spokes in the form of seasons; चक्रे (*cakre*)—in the wheel in the form of the year; परिवर्तमाने (*parivartamāne*)—which revolves again and again in the forms of the saṃvatsara, parivatsara and so on; तस्मिन् (*tasmin*)—in the wheel of time; विश्वा (*viśvā*)—all; भुवनानि (*bhuvanāni*)—the worlds; आ तस्थुः (*ā tasthuḥ*)—rest; तस्य (*tasya*)—of this wheel, that which is in the middle, भूरिभारः (*bhūribhāraḥ*)—which bears an abundant burden: अक्षः (*akṣaḥ*)—the axle of the chariot; न तप्यते (*na tapyate*)—is not obstructed *[the Kannada word is "ಕುಂಠಿತವಾಗುವುದಿಲ್ಲ", "is not blunted"]*; सनादेव (*sanādeva*)—even though extremely ancient; सनाभिः (*sanābhiḥ*)—its one and only nave (centre); न शीर्यते (*na śīryate*)—is not worn away.

### Printed p. 369
*Running head: Ṛgveda-saṃhitā 369 [ಆ. ೨. ಅ. ೩. ವ. ೧೬.] (as supplied: "ಆ." at the start).*

**भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)**
In the wheel in the form of the year, furnished with five spokes in the form of seasons, in this wheel of time which revolves again and again in the forms of the saṃvatsara, parivatsara and so on, all the worlds rest. The axle of the chariot, which is in the middle of this wheel of time and bears an abundant burden, is not obstructed at all; although extremely ancient, its one and only nave is not worn away.

*[English Trauslation]* *(garbled label as supplied; repaired by the script to "English Translation.")*

**Printed English**
All beings abide in this five-spoked revolving wheel; the heavily-loaded axle is never heated ; its eternal compact nave is never worn away.

**विशेषविषयगळु (Viśeṣaviṣayagaḷu)**
In this Ṛk the nature of the wheel of time, which is without beginning, supports the universe and is free from decay, is described. In the pāda पंचारे चक्रे (*paṃcāre cakre*) परिवर्तमाने (*parivartamāne*) तस्मिन् (*tasmin*) the word पंचारे (*paṃcāre*) is an epithet of the wheel of time, "belonging to the year, furnished with spokes in the form of the five seasons": Sāyaṇa's words are given in the Kannada as "ಪಂಚಯತು ರೂಪೈಃ ಆರೈಃ ಯುಕ್ತೇ" *[as supplied: the print has पंचयतु (*paṃcayatu*), broken across the line, where the sense requires "five seasons"; the words रूपैः आरैः युक्ते (*rūpaiḥ āraiḥ yukte*) follow]*. That the number of the seasons becomes five if the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons are reckoned as one because of the likeness of their qualities, Sāyaṇa explained in the previous Ṛk with the sentence "एतत् हेमंत शिशिरयोः एकत्वाभिप्रायं (*etat hemaṃta śiśirayoḥ ekatvābhiprāyaṃ*)". And that Śaṅkara and others have stated this view was shown earlier by quoting the Praśna Upaniṣad sentence.

Besides, पंचारे चक्रे (*paṃcāre cakre*) may also be explained from a spiritual point of view. Since the whole universe is fivefold (pāṅkta), and since the fivefold universe rests in the beginningless wheel of time, this description may explain that point also. In the Taittirīya Upaniṣad its explanation is given in this manner:

पृथिवी अंतरिक्षं द्यौः दिशः अवांतरदिशाः अग्निः वायुः आदित्यः चंद्रमा नक्षत्राणि आस ओषधयो वनस्पतय आकाश आत्मा इत्यधिभूतं (*pṛthivī aṃtarikṣaṃ dyauḥ diśaḥ avāṃtaradiśāḥ agniḥ vāyuḥ ādityaḥ caṃdramā nakṣatrāṇi āsa oṣadhayo vanaspataya ākāśa ātmā ityadhibhūtaṃ*)

All these are the fivefold group relating to the elements (ādhibhautika): "thus the adhibhūta". अथाध्यात्मं (*athādhyātmaṃ*)—now the spiritual fivefold group will be explained—

| प्राणो (*prāṇo*) | व्यानो (*vyāno*) | अपान (*apāna*) | उदानः (*udānaḥ*) | समानः (*samānaḥ*) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| चक्षुः (*cakṣuḥ*) | श्रोत्रं (*śrotraṃ*) | मनो (*mano*) | नाक् (*nāk*) *[as supplied]* | त्वक् (*tvak*) |
| चर्म (*carma*) | मांसं (*māṃsaṃ*) | स्नाना (*snānā*) *[as supplied]* | अस्थि (*asthi*) | मज्जा (*majjā*) |

*(The foot of the page carries the signature mark "[24] [Vol. 12" as supplied.)*

### Printed p. 370
*Running head: 370 Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā [ ಮಂ. ೧. ಅ. ೨೨. ಸೂ. ೧೬೪] (as supplied).*

All these are the vital airs beginning with prāṇa, the fivefold group of the senses beginning with the eye, and the fivefold group of the bodily constituents beginning with skin. एतदधिविधाय ऋषिरवोचत् । पांक्तं वा इदग्ं सर्वं । पांक्तेनैव पांक्तग्स् स्पृणोतीति (*etadadhividhāya ṛṣiravocat | pāṃktaṃ vā idagṃ sarvaṃ | pāṃktenaiva pāṃktags spṛṇotīti*)
(Tai. U. 1-2 *[as supplied: "ತೈ. ಉ."]*)

The sage has said in the above sentence that all the material and spiritual parts of the universe are thus fivefold. Since it is explained that the activity of the universe is by the union of these two fivefold groups, this fivefold group too, which is of the nature of a wheel, is contained in the wheel of time itself. पंचारे चक्रे (*paṃcāre cakre*) तस्मिन् (*tasmin*) can be explained from this point of view too.

परिवर्तमाने (*parivartamāne*)—संवत्सरपरिवत्सरादिरूपेण पुनः पुनः आवर्तमाने सति (*saṃvatsaraparivatsarādirūpeṇa punaḥ punaḥ āvartamāne sati*). It is an epithet of the wheel of time: "revolving again and again in the forms of the saṃvatsara, parivatsara and so on". There was a custom of calling the wheel of time by five names, संवत्सर, परिवत्सर, इदावत्सर, इद्वत्सर (*saṃvatsara, parivatsara, idāvatsara, idvatsara*) and वत्सर (*vatsara*). Small differences are seen here and there both in these names and in their reckoning. For example, in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā:

यत्ते रुद्र पुरो धनुस्तद्वातो अनु वातु ते तस्मै ते रुद्र संवत्सरेण नमस्करोमि (*yatte rudra puro dhanustadvāto anu vātu te tasmai te rudra saṃvatsareṇa namaskaromi*)

यत्ते रुद्र दक्षिणाधनुः (*yatte rudra dakṣiṇādhanuḥ*) (the following words repeated, as the print shows by ditto marks ",,") परिवत्सरेण (*parivatsareṇa*) (",,");
यत्ते रुद्रॆ पश्चाद्दनुः (*yatte rudrè paścāddanuḥ*) (the same, ",,") इदावत्सरेण (*idāvatsareṇa*) (",,");
यत्ते रुद्रोत्तराद्दनुः (*yatte rudrottarāddanuḥ*) (the same, ",,") इदुवत्सरेण (*iduvatsareṇa*) (",,");
यत्ते रुद्रोपरि धनुः (*yatte rudropari dhanuḥ*) (the same, ",,") वत्सरेण (*vatsareṇa*) (",,").

In these sentences the varieties are saṃvatsara, parivatsara, idāvatsara, iduvatsara and vatsara. The same division is found in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā also (Vā. Saṃ. 27-45). But there, in place of इद्वत्सर (*idvatsara*), the Taittirīya Saṃhitā has इदुवत्सर (*iduvatsara*) *[as supplied: this is how the Kannada states the difference]*. The rest are the same. In the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa:

संवत्सरोऽसि परिवत्सरोऽसि । इदावत्सरोऽसीदुवत्सरोऽसि । इद्वत्सरोऽसि वत्सरोऽसि । तस्य ते वसंतश्शिरः । ग्रीष्मो दक्षिणः पक्षः (*saṃvatsaro 'si parivatsaro 'si | idāvatsaro 'sīduvatsaro 'si | idvatsaro 'si vatsaro 'si | tasya te vasaṃtaśśiraḥ | grīṣmo dakṣiṇaḥ pakṣaḥ*)
*[as supplied: "ಕೈ. ಬ್ರಾ. 3-10-4-1"; the dotted gaps are in the print]*

There are six varieties: saṃvatsara, parivatsara, idāvatsara, iduvatsara, idvatsara and vatsara. But in this same Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa,

### Printed p. 371
*Running head: Ṛgveda-saṃhitā 371 [ಅ.೨.ಅ. ೩ ವ. ೧೬. ] (as supplied).*

अग्निर्वाव संवत्सरः । आदित्यः परिवत्सरः (*agnirvāva saṃvatsaraḥ | ādityaḥ parivatsaraḥ*)
(Tai. Brā. 1-4-10-1 *[as supplied: "ತೈ. ಬ್ರಾ"]*)

here only four varieties are mentioned: saṃvatsara, parivatsara, idāvatsara and anuvatsara. Besides, in another part of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā:

इदुवथ्सराय परिवत्सराय संवथ्सराय कृणुता बृहन्नमः (*iduvathsarāya parivatsarāya saṃvathsarāya kṛṇutā bṛhannamaḥ*)
(Tai. Saṃ. 5-7-2-4)

only three varieties are mentioned: iduvatsara, parivatsara and saṃvatsara. In all these sentences the two names saṃvatsara and parivatsara are common. It is described that the wheel of time has been revolving like a wheel in these forms from beginningless time.

तस्मिन्नातस्थुर्भुवनानि विश्वा (*tasminnātasthurbhuvanāni viśvā*)—the meaning is that all the worlds rest in this wheel of time. Names such as saṃvatsara and parivatsara are the limbs of this Great Time. This Great Time itself is the support of the world and of all the activities of the world. This very thing is called by many names such as svabhāva (own nature), niyama (law) and Brahman.

किं कारणं, ब्रह्म ? कुतः स्म जाता जीवाम केन क्व च संप्रतिष्ठाः । अधिष्ठिताः केन सुखेतरेषु वर्तामहे ब्रह्मविदो व्यवस्थां (*kiṃ kāraṇaṃ, brahma ? kutaḥ sma jātā jīvāma kena kva ca saṃpratiṣṭhāḥ | adhiṣṭhitāḥ kena sukhetareṣu vartāmahe brahmavido vyavasthāṃ*)
(Śve. U. 1-1 *[as supplied: "ಶ್ವೇ. ಉ."]*)

What is the original cause of the world? Is it Brahman? Or what is Brahman? What is its nature? From where is our origin? By the support of what do we live? What is the basis of our existence? From where do our pleasures and pains arise? To the question there is this kind of answer:

कालः स्वभावो नियतिर्यदृच्छा भूतानि योनिः पुरुष इति चिंत्या (*kālaḥ svabhāvo niyatiryadṛcchā bhūtāni yoniḥ puruṣa iti ciṃtyā*)
*[as supplied: "ಶ್ವೇ. ಉ" cut off, and then "ಶ್ರೀ. ಉ. ೧-೨"; read as Sve. U. 1-2, the reference being printed twice, the first broken]*

Some call this great origin of the world Time, some Niyati (fate), some Svabhāva (own nature); in the same way different knowers of the truth call it by some other names. But:

स्वभावमेके कवयो वदंति कालं तथान्ये परिमुह्यमानाः । देवस्यैष महिमा तु लोके येनेदं भ्राम्यते बह्मचक्रं (*svabhāvameke kavayo vadaṃti kālaṃ tathānye parimuhyamānāḥ | devasyaiṣa mahimā tu loke yenedaṃ bhrāmyate bahmacakraṃ*)
*[as supplied: "ಕ್ವೆಂ. ಉ. ೬-೧", presumably the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad; the abbreviation is odd and is reported; the last word is printed बह्मचक्रं (*bahmacakraṃ*)]*

Some poets call this great origin Svabhāva, others call it Time. By this the nature of it is not fully described. He who, having established all the worlds by his power, also causes the Brahma-wheel to revolve

### Printed p. 372
*Running head: 372 Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā [ಮಂ. ೧. ಅ. ೨೨. ಸೂ. ೧೬೪] (as supplied).*

is the Supreme Person, Īśvara. It is described that by him the Brahma-wheel, the cause of the world, also is made to revolve. The description of the wheel of time given in the present passage is to be understood as the primal principle described under different names. Whatever sage, by whatever name he may call this primal principle, no other fitting likeness can be given to this primal cause except by comparing it to the wheel of a chariot. Whether it be called Ātman, Brahman or Niyati, the relation it has to the world of activity must be compared to the relation of the wheel of a chariot to its spokes. The method of describing the primal principle by showing that comparison can be seen generally in all the Upaniṣads. For example, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad:

स वा अयमात्मा सर्वेषां भूतानामधिपतिः सर्वेषां भूतानां राजा तद्यथा रथनाभौ च रथनेमौ चाराः सर्वे समर्पिता एवमेवास्मिन्नात्मनि सर्वाणि भूतानि सर्वे देवाः सर्वे लोकाः सर्वे प्राणाः सर्व एवात्मनः समर्पिताः (*sa vā ayamātmā sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāmadhipatiḥ sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ rājā tadyathā rathanābhau ca rathanemau cārāḥ sarve samarpitā evamevāsminnātmani sarvāṇi bhūtāni sarve devāḥ sarve lokāḥ sarve prāṇāḥ sarva evātmanaḥ samarpitāḥ*)
(Bṛ. U. 2-5-15)

This Ātman is the lord of all beings. As all the spokes are contained in the nave and the felly of the chariot wheel and have fixed positions, so all beings are contained in this Ātman and are subject to this Ātman's control. All beings, all deities, all worlds, all vital airs, everything, are offered to the control of this Ātman and depend on it; thus a likeness is stated between this Soul of the world and a chariot wheel. Similarly in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad and in the Praśna Upaniṣad also:

अरा इव रथनाभौ संहता यत्र नाड्यः स एषोऽंतश्चरते बहुधा जायमानः (*arā iva rathanābhau saṃhatā yatra nāḍyaḥ sa eṣo 'ṃtaścarate bahudhā jāyamānaḥ*)
(Mu. 2-2-6 *[as supplied: "ಮು."]*)

आरा इव रथनाभौ प्राणे सर्वं प्रतिष्ठितं । यजो यजूग्ंषि सामानि यज्ञः क्षत्रं ब्रह्म च (*ārā iva rathanābhau prāṇe sarvaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ | yajo yajūgṃṣi sāmāni yajñaḥ kṣatraṃ brahma ca*)
(Praśna 2-6 *[as supplied: "ಪ್ರಶ್ನ."]*)

अरा इव रथनाभौ कला यस्मिन्प्रतिष्ठिताः । तं वेद्यं पुरुषं वेद यथा मा वो मृत्युः परिव्यथा इति (*arā iva rathanābhau kalā yasminpratiṣṭhitāḥ | taṃ vedyaṃ puruṣaṃ veda yathā mā vo mṛtyuḥ parivyathā iti*)
(Praśna 6-6 *[as supplied: "ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆ."]*)

### Printed p. 373
*Running head: Ṛgveda-saṃhitā 373 [ಅ. ೨. ಅ. ೩. ವ. ೧೬. ] (as supplied).*

Thus the relation of the individual soul to all the parts of the living being, the relation of the vital air to the Ṛk and the rest, and the relation of the Primal Person to all the kalās are compared to the relation of the nave of a chariot to its spokes. Therefore, although in the present Ṛk this great principle is described as the wheel of time, it must be understood to be the primal principle described elsewhere by names such as Brahman and Ātman. For that very reason the description in the second half of this Ṛk describes also its being without beginning and without end. In the same way, in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad this one principle is compared to a wheel, and the various parts of the universe, which are its constituents, to the parts of the wheel:

तमेकनेमिं त्रिवृतं षोडशांतं शतार्धारं विंशतिप्रत्यराभिः । अष्टकैः षड्भर्विश्वरूपैकपाशं त्रिमार्गभेदं द्विनिमित्तैकमोहं (*tamekanemiṃ trivṛtaṃ ṣoḍaśāṃtaṃ śatārdhāraṃ viṃśatipratyarābhiḥ | aṣṭakaiḥ ṣaḍbharviśvarūpaikapāśaṃ trimārgabhedaṃ dvinimittaikamohaṃ*)
(Śve. U. 1-4)

It is described that this one principle, the Soul of the universe, has a single felly, त्रिवृतवू (*trivṛtavū*) (threefold), sixteen at the end, fifty spokes, twenty counter-spokes, six groups of eight, one noose binding the whole universe, three paths, and one delusion with two causes. The threefold here is the three qualities, sattva, rajas and tamas; the five organs of knowledge, the five organs of action and the mind, together with the five elements, make up the sixteen (16).

एष प्रत्ययसर्गो विपर्ययाशक्तितुष्टि सिद्धाख्यः । गुणवैषम्यविमर्दात् तस्य च भेदास्तु पंचाशत् (*eṣa pratyayasargo viparyayāśaktituṣṭi siddhākhyaḥ | guṇavaiṣamyavimardāt tasya ca bhedāstu paṃcāśat*)
(Sāṃkhyakārikā 46)

As explained in this verse, "pratyaya-sarga" means ignorance; viparyaya (error), aśakti (incapacity), tuṣṭi (contentment) and siddhi (perfection) with their subdivisions are fifty kinds. These are compared to the fifty spokes, सतार्धारं (*satārdhāraṃ*) (100/2) *[as supplied: सतार्धारं (*satārdhāraṃ*) with the figure "೧೦೦/೨"; the verse above reads शतार्धारं (*śatārdhāraṃ*)]*. Giving the likeness of the counter-spokes, which are like warp and woof to these, the five organs of knowledge and the five organs of action, together with the ten objects corresponding to them, are compared to the twenty counter-spokes. अष्टकैष्षड्भिः (*aṣṭakaiṣṣaḍbhiḥ*) means: the six groups of eight. They are:

1) The five elements, the mind, the intellect and egoism, these eight together make the first group. Similarly,

2) the eight constituents of the body; *(the list continues in the next window; the window ends here as supplied)*

### Printed p. 374
*Running head: 374 ಸಾಯಣಭಾಷ್ಯಸಹಿತಾ [ಮಂ. ೧. ಅ. ೨೨. ಸೂ. ೧೬೪] (as supplied).*

(Continuing the list of the six groups of eight:)

3) the eight impersonal (apauruṣeya) powers; 4) the eight bhāvas (states); 5) the eight deities; 6) the eight guṇas (qualities). The collection of these is described as अष्टकैष्कड्डिः (*aṣṭakaiṣkaḍḍiḥ*) *[as supplied: so spelt here; the earlier passage has a different spelling of the same word]*. Further, desire (kāma) is called the rope of this chariot, and dharma, adharma and knowledge are called the three tracks of the chariot-wheel. In the same manner, comparing the principle of the universe to the wheel of a chariot, and the various parts of the universe to the different members of the wheel, is a common feature of the Śruti texts. Likewise in the present Ṛk also it is described: पंचारे चक्रे परिवर्तमाने तस्मिन्नातस्थुर्भुवनानि विश्वा (*paṃcāre cakre parivartamāne tasminnātasthurbhuvanāni viśvā*). In this wheel of the universe, which is of the nature of Time, the parts such as the vatsara and the parivatsara revolve again and again and are subject to old age and death; yet this original principle alone remains eternal. Therefore its imperishable state is described by नाक्षस्तप्यते (*nākṣastapyate*) ; सनादेव शीर्यते सनाभिः (*sanādeva śīryate sanābhiḥ*). Because it carries the whole burden of the universe, its axle bears a very great load, and yet it does not become blunted. This wheel of the universe, which is of the nature of Time, may be compared to the Agni, the Vāyu and the Sūrya described in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad *[as supplied: the Kannada spells the Upaniṣad's name ಕಠೋಪತಿಷತ್ತಿನಲ್ಲಿ, and "Sūra" ಸೂರ for the sun]*.

अग्निर्यथैको भुवनं प्रविष्टो रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूव । एकस्तथा सर्व भूतांतरात्मा रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बहिश्च ॥ (*agniryathaiko bhuvanaṃ praviṣṭo rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva | ekastathā sarva bhūtāṃtarātmā rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo bahiśca ‖*)

सूर्यो यथा सर्वलोकस्य चक्षुर्न लिप्यते चाक्षुषैर्बाह्यदोषैः । एकस्तथा सर्वभूतांतरात्मा न लिप्यते लोकदुःखेन बाह्यः ॥ (*sūryo yathā sarvalokasya cakṣurna lipyate cākṣuṣairbāhyadoṣaiḥ | ekastathā sarvabhūtāṃtarātmā na lipyate lokaduḥkhena bāhyaḥ ‖*)

(Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5-9-11)

In the manner in which the one single principle spreads in the universe and takes the form of every object, in the same manner this principle of Time also, pervading the universe, takes on the individual measure of each thing. But in the manner in which the sun, the eye of the whole world, is not tainted by the external defects of the eye that beholds him, in the same way this principle of Time is not tainted by the defects of the individual world. It is neither perishable; it is eternal and steady.

यथा लौकिकरथाक्षः भारेण भग्नो भवति अक्षघातेन च नाभिर्विवृता भवति तद्वदत्रापि नास्तीत्यर्थः ॥ (*yathā laukikarathākṣaḥ bhāreṇa bhagno bhavati akṣaghātena ca nābhirvivṛtā bhavati tadvadatrāpi nāstītyarthaḥ ‖*)

In the manner in which the axle of a worldly chariot breaks by carrying a burden beyond its strength, and thereby its nave becomes deformed, so, even though it carries the burden of the universe, so the axle of this chariot-wheel *(the sentence is cut by the page end and continues on p. 375)*.

### Printed p. 375
*Running head: [ಆ. ೨. ಆ. ೩. ವ. ೧೬ ] ಋಗ್ವೇದಸಂಹಿತಾ 375 (as supplied).*

(Continuing) ...and so the axle of this wheel does not break even though it bears the burden of the universe, and its nave does not become deformed; thus Sāyaṇa has explained the purport of the second half.

*Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā (grammatical derivation)*

परिवर्तमाने (*parivartamāne*)—from the root वृतु वर्तने (*vṛtu vartane*); for लट् (*laṭ*) the substitute शानचादेश (*śānacādeśa*). By the rule पुगंतलघूपधस्यच (*pugaṃtalaghūpadhasyaca*) (Pā. Sū. 7-3-86), after the vikaraṇa śap, guṇa for the laghūpadha of the root. By तास्यनुदात्तेत् (*tāsyanudāttet*) (Pā. Sū. (6-1-186) *[as supplied: the reference is printed with the bracket opened twice, "(ಪಾ.ಸೂ." at the line end and "(೬-೧-೧೮೬)" on the next line]*, since the लसार्वधातुकवु (*lasārvadhātukavu*) becomes anudātta, the accent of the root remains. In the Prādi compound, the accent of the prakṛti of the latter member (kṛd-uttarapada-prakṛti-svara) comes.

विश्वा (*viśvā*)—in the neuter plural, by शेश्छंदसि बहुलं (*śeśchaṃdasi bahulaṃ*) (Pā Sū. 6-1-70) *[as supplied: "ಪಾ ಸೂ." without the full stop]* elision of śi.

तप्यते (*tapyate*)—the root तप संतापे (*tapa saṃtāpe*). A form ending in the passive Present (लट् (*laṭ*)), third person singular. The tiṅanta-nighāta accent comes.

भूरिभारः (*bhūribhāraḥ*)—भूरि भारः यस्य सः (*bhūri bhāraḥ yasya saḥ*) (he of whom the burden is great); in the bahuvrīhi the accent of the prakṛti of the former member comes.

शीर्यते (*śīryate*)—the root श्य हिंसायां (*śya hiṃsāyāṃ*) *[as supplied: root spelt so]*. Passive Present (लट् (*laṭ*)). By सार्वधातुके यक् (*sārvadhātuke yak*) (Pā. Sū. 3-1-67), when yak has come, by ऋत इद्दातोः (*ṛta iddātoḥ*) the root takes i (ittva); when r follows, lengthening. The tiṅanta-nighāta accent comes.

सनाभिः (*sanābhiḥ*)—समानः नाभिः यस्य सः सनाभिः (*samānaḥ nābhiḥ yasya saḥ sanābhiḥ*); by समानस्य छंदस्यमूर्ध (*samānasya chaṃdasyamūrdha*)- (Pā. Sū. 6-3-84) the substitution sa for the word samāna; in the bahuvrīhi the accent of the prakṛti of the former member comes. (End of Ṛk 13; printed ‖ 13 ‖.)

#### Ṛk 14
**॥ संहितापाठः ॥**
> सने॑मि च॒क्रम॒जरं॒ वि वा॑वृत उत्ता॒नायां॒ दश॑ यु॒क्ता॑
> वहंति ।
> सूर्य॑स्य॒ चक्षू॒ रज॑सै॒त्यावृ॑तं॒ तस्मि॒न्नार्पि॑ता॒ भुव॑नानि॒ विश्वा॑ ॥
> ॥ १४ ॥
**॥ पदपाठः ॥**

### Printed p. 376
*Running head: 376 ಸಾಯಣಭಾಷ್ಯಸಹಿತಾ [ ಮಂ. ೧. ಆ. ೨೨. ಸೂ. ೧೬೪] (as supplied).* *[as supplied: "ಆ. ೨೨" for the Anuvāka here, against "ಅ. ೨೨" on p. 374]*

**॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥**
> सनेमि समाननेम्येकप्रकारबहिर्वलयमक्षीणनेमि चक्रं संवत्सराख्यमजरं
> सदातनमपि जरारहितं वि ववृते । पुनःपुनर्विशेषेण वर्तते । उत्तानायामूर्ध्वतनायामीषायामुपरिविस्त्रतभूम्यां वा दशेंद्रादयः पंच लोकपाला
> निषादपंच-माश्चत्वारो ब्राह्मणादयो वर्णा मिलित्वा दशसंख्याका युक्ताः
> स्वस्वव्यापारयुक्ता वहंति । निर्वहंति । कृत्स्नं जगन्निर्वहंतीत्यर्थः । तन्निर्वाहार्थत्वात्कालस्य । किंच सूर्यस्यादित्यस्य चक्षुः ख्यानस्वभावं सर्वस्य चक्षुःस्थानीयं
> वा मंडलं । चक्षुः ख्यातेर्वा चष्टेर्वति निरुक्तं । ४-३ । रजसा वृष्टु दकेनावृतं
> व्याप्तमेति । गच्छति । उदकं रज उच्यत इति यास्कः । नि ४-१९ । तादृशे मंडले विश्वा
> भुवनानि सर्वाणि भूतजातान्यार्पिता । अर्पितानि । तदधीनत्वात्तेषां ॥
*Gist:* The year-wheel, undecaying, revolves; ten (five world-guardians and five classes of men) bear it; the sun's orb, invested with water, moves; all beings rest in it.

**प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)**
सनेमि (*sanemi*)—(never wearing out) having an outer rim of one uniform kind; अजरं (*ajaraṃ*)—imperishable; चक्रं (*cakraṃ*)—this wheel of the universe; वि ववृते (*vi vavṛte*)—revolves again and again; उत्तानायां (*uttānāyāṃ*)—in its upper part; दश (*daśa*)—the five guardians of the worlds beginning with Indra, and the men of the Brāhmaṇa and other classes, with the Niṣāda as the fifth; युक्ता (*yuktā*)—engaged in their respective appointed duties; वहंति (*vahaṃti*)—carry out the work of the world; सूरस्य (*sūrasya*)—of Sūra *[as supplied: the Kannada word is so printed; the verse reads सूर्यस्य (*sūryasya*)]*, सूरन (*sūrana*) *[as supplied: "of the sun"]*; चक्षुः (*cakṣuḥ*)—the orb, which is of the form of the eye of the world; रजसा (*rajasā*)—with water; आवृतं (*āvṛtaṃ*)—pervaded; एति (*eti*)—moves about; तस्मिन् (*tasmin*)—(universe-pervading) in that orb; विश्वा भुवनानि (*viśvā bhuvanāni*)—all the worlds; अर्पिता (*arpitā*)—are deposited.

**भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)**
This wheel of the universe, which has a uniform outer rim and is imperishable, revolves again and again. In its upper part the five world-guardians beginning with Indra, and men of the five classes, each engaged in his own appointed duty, carry out the work of the world. The orb of the sun, the eye of the world, moves pervaded by water; in that all-pervading orb all the worlds are deposited (established).

**Printed English**
The even-fellied, undecaying wheel, repeatedly revolves: ten, united on the upper surface, bear (the world): the orb of the sun proceeds, invested with water, and in it are all beings deposited.

### Printed p. 377
*Running head: [ಅ. ೨. ಅ. ೩. ವ. ೧೬. ] ಋಗ್ವೇದಸಂಹಿತಾ 377 (as supplied).*

**विशेषविषयगळु (Viśeṣaviṣayagaḷu)**

Although the idea of the preceding Ṛk is the very same one stated in this Ṛk, the special point here is the description that the activity of the world proceeds in an unbroken sequence in subjection to the governance of this wheel of the universe. In this context the identity of the wheel of Time and the orb of the sun is shown. It has been stated before that from one point of view the revolution of the sun depends on Time, and from another point of view the comings and goings of Time depend on the sun. Here, and in the preceding Ṛk, the non-difference of the two is indicated, and it is said that the activity of the guardians of the worlds, Indra and the others, is also dependent on it. This same idea is stated in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka in this manner:

यस्मादर्नाक्संवत्सरोऽहोभिः परिवर्तते । तद्देवा ज्योतीषां ज्योतिरायुर्होपासतेmृतं ॥ (*yasmādarnāksaṃvatsaro 'hobhiḥ parivartate | taddevā jyotīṣāṃ jyotirāyurhopāsatemṛtaṃ ‖*) *[as supplied: the Latin letter "m" stands inside the Kannada word]*

(Bṛ. U. 4-4-16)

In this sentence are stated the points described in the present Ṛk: सनेमि चक्रमजरं वि ववृते (*sanemi cakramajaraṃ vi vavṛte*) and सूरस्य चक्षुरेति (*sūrasya cakṣureti*). Śaṅkarācārya has commented on this sentence as follows:

संवत्सरः कालात्मा सर्वस्य जनिमतः परिच्छेत्ता यमपरिच्छिंदन्नर्वागेव वर्ततेऽहोभिः स्वावयवैरहोरात्रैरित्यर्थः । तज्योतीषां ज्योतिः ॥ (*saṃvatsaraḥ kālātmā sarvasya janimataḥ paricchettā yamaparicchiṃdannarvāgeva vartate 'hobhiḥ svāvayavairahorātrairityarthaḥ | tajyotīṣāṃ jyotiḥ ‖*)

On the strength of this original principle, the year and the others, maintaining their revolution of recurrence, carry on the affairs of the world. Having explained the original principle, the support of the activity of the universe, as "that which has a splendour greater than all splendours", he then goes on:

यस्मिन्पंच पंचजना आकाशश्च प्रतिष्ठितः । तमेव मन्य आत्मानं विद्वान्ब्रह्मामृतोऽमृतं ॥ (*yasminpaṃca paṃcajanā ākāśaśca pratiṣṭhitaḥ | tameva manya ātmānaṃ vidvānbrahmāmṛto 'mṛtaṃ ‖*)

(Bṛ. U. 4-4-17)

In this verse the matter stated in the present Ṛk, उत्तानायां दश युक्ता वहंति (*uttānāyāṃ daśa yuktā vahaṃti*), is conveyed. Commenting on it, Śaṅkarācārya says:

किंच यस्मिन्ब्रह्मणि (*kiṃca yasminbrahmaṇi*) (it was stated before that this original principle is called by many names such as Time, Nature, Destiny, Brahman). पंच पंचजना गंधर्वादयः पंचैव संख्याका गंधर्वाः पितरो देवा असुरा रक्षांसि निषादपंचमा वा वर्णा आकाशश्चाव्याकृताख्यो यस्मिन्सूत्रमोतं च प्रोतं च यस्मिन्प्रतिष्ठितः ॥ (*paṃca paṃcajanā gaṃdharvādayaḥ paṃcaiva saṃkhyākā gaṃdharvāḥ pitaro devā asurā rakṣāṃsi niṣādapaṃcamā vā varṇā ākāśaścāvyākṛtākhyo yasminsūtramotaṃ ca protaṃ ca yasminpratiṣṭhitaḥ ‖*)

On the strength of this original principle the group of the gods numbering five, beginning with the Gandharvas, and the human group of five classes, carry on their respective activities. In it the whole universe is woven together like warp and woof (ota and prota). Explaining this very point to Gārgī, Yājñavalkya says:

### Printed p. 378
*Running head: 378 ಸಾಯಣಭಾಷ್ಯಸಹಿತಾ [ಮಂ. ೧. ಅ. ೨೨. ಸೂ. ೧೬೪.] (as supplied).*

एतस्य वा अक्षरस्य प्रशासने गार्गि सूर्याचंद्रमसौ विधृतौ तिष्ठत एतस्य वा अक्षरस्य प्रशासने गार्गि द्यावापृथिव्यौ विधृते तिष्ठत एतस्य वा अक्षरस्य प्रशासने गार्गि निमेषा मुहूर्ता अहोरात्राण्यर्धमासा मासा ऋतवः संवत्सरा इति विधृतास्तिष्ठंत्येतस्य वा अक्षरस्य प्रशासने गार्गि प्राज्योऽन्या नद्यः स्यंदंते श्वेतेभ्यः पर्वतेभ्यः प्रतीच्योऽन्यायां यां यां च दिशमन्वेतस्य वा अक्षरस्य प्रशासने गार्गि ददतो मनुष्याः प्रशंसंति यजमानं देवा दर्वि० पितरोन्वायत्ताः ॥ (*etasya vā akṣarasya praśāsane gārgi sūryācaṃdramasau vidhṛtau tiṣṭhata etasya vā akṣarasya praśāsane gārgi dyāvāpṛthivyau vidhṛte tiṣṭhata etasya vā akṣarasya praśāsane gārgi nimeṣā muhūrtā ahorātrāṇyardhamāsā māsā ṛtavaḥ saṃvatsarā iti vidhṛtāstiṣṭhaṃtyetasya vā akṣarasya praśāsane gārgi prājyo 'nyā nadyaḥ syaṃdaṃte śvetebhyaḥ parvatebhyaḥ pratīcyo 'nyāyāṃ yāṃ yāṃ ca diśamanvetasya vā akṣarasya praśāsane gārgi dadato manuṣyāḥ praśaṃsaṃti yajamānaṃ devā darvi0 pitaronvāyattāḥ ‖*)

(Bṛ. U. 3-8-9)

O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable (described in the present Ṛk as "ajara", undecaying) the sun and the moon stand in their fixed places. Heaven and earth do not transgress their bounds *[as supplied: the Kannada word is मारुवुदिल्ल (*māruvudilla*), literally "do not sell"; the sense requires "transgress"]*. Moments, muhūrtas, days-and-nights, half-months, months, seasons and years appear and disappear within their limits. By the command of this Imperishable the streams of rivers and the like also flow.

एतस्मिन्नु खल्वक्षरे गार्ग्याकाश ओतश्च प्रोतश्चेति ॥ (*etasminnu khalvakṣare gārgyākāśa otaśca protaśceti ‖*)

(Bṛ. U. 3-8-11)

In the Imperishable the whole world, beginning with space, is gathered together like warp and woof. Besides this:

भीषास्माद्वातः पवते । भीषोदेति सूर्यः । भीषास्मादग्निश्चंद्रश्च । (*bhīṣāsmādvātaḥ pavate | bhīṣodeti sūryaḥ | bhīṣāsmādagniścaṃdraśca |*)

(Tai. U. 2-8-1)

Only in obedience to the command of this great principle do the wind, the sun, the fire and Indra carry out their respective appointed duties; thus, praising the power of this Imperishable in many Śruti texts, it is declared that the entire activity of the world depends on it.

दश युक्ता वहंति (*daśa yuktā vahaṃti*)—the total meaning of this sentence has been explained above. But since other meanings are possible for the word दश (*daśa*), it must be examined what meanings can be given to this word in the present context on the strength of Śruti texts. Sāyaṇa, explaining it, says:

इंद्रादयः पंच लोकपालाः निषादपंचमाश्चत्वारो ब्राह्मणादयो वर्णाः मिळित्वा दशसंख्याकाः ॥ (*iṃdrādayaḥ paṃca lokapālāḥ niṣādapaṃcamāścatvāro brāhmaṇādayo varṇāḥ miḷitvā daśasaṃkhyākāḥ ‖*)

He has explained it as the five guardians of the worlds beginning with Indra, and men of the five classes. Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Soma and Brahmā are the five well known as the guardians of the worlds. Explaining the word पंचजनाः (*paṃcajanāḥ*), the author of the Nirukta says *(the quotation continues on the next page)*.

### Printed p. 379
*Running head: [ಅ ೨. ಅ. ೩. ವ. ೧೬.] ಋಗ್ವೇದಸಂಹಿತಾ 379 (as supplied).*

पंजजना (मम होत्रं जुषध्वं) गंधर्वाः पितरो देवा असुरा रक्षांसीत्येके ! चत्वारो वर्णा निषादः पंचम इत्यौपमन्यवः ॥ (*paṃjajanā (mama hotraṃ juṣadhvaṃ) gaṃdharvāḥ pitaro devā asurā rakṣāṃsītyeke ! catvāro varṇā niṣādaḥ paṃcama ityaupamanyavaḥ ‖*) *[as supplied: the first word is printed पंजजना (*paṃjajanā*); and "!" stands for the danda]*

He has stated that, according to some, the five kinds of people are the Gandharvas, the Pitṛs, the gods, the Asuras and the Rākṣasas; and that Aupamanyava and others hold that the four classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, together with the Niṣādas as the fifth group, make up the five peoples. Formerly, when all the gods addressed Agni, praying that he should receive the oblation offered in the sacrifice for them and distribute it to all, Agni agreed to it, and:

तदद्य वाचः प्रथमं मसीय येनासुरा अभि देवा असाम । ऊर्जाद उत यज्ञियासः पंच जना मम होत्रं जुषध्वं ॥ (*tadadya vācaḥ prathamaṃ masīya yenāsurā abhi devā asāma | ūrjāda uta yajñiyāsaḥ paṃca janā mama hotraṃ juṣadhvaṃ ‖*)

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-53-4)

The author of the Bṛhaddevatā quotes this sentence, in which the answer was given that the five peoples may enjoy this oblation, shows the differences of opinion as to who the five peoples are, and discusses them.

प्रत्युवाचाथ तानग्निर्विश्वेदेवा यदूच मां । तत्करिष्ये जुषंतां तु होत्रं पंचजना मम ॥ (*pratyuvācātha tānagnirviśvedevā yadūca māṃ | tatkariṣye juṣaṃtāṃ tu hotraṃ paṃcajanā mama ‖*)

(Bṛ. De. 6-96)

In this verse the answer that Agni gave to the gods is stated, and then the word पंचजन (*paṃcajana*) is explained:

शालामुख्यः प्रणीतश्च पुत्रो गृहपतेश्च यः । उत्तरो दक्षिणश्चाग्निरेते पंचजनाः स्मृताः ॥ (*śālāmukhyaḥ praṇītaśca putro gṛhapateśca yaḥ | uttaro dakṣiṇaścāgnirete paṃcajanāḥ smṛtāḥ ‖*)

(Bṛ. De. 7-67)

That is: the fire at the entrance of the hall, the consecrated Āhavanīya fire, the Gārhapatya fire which is the son of the sacrificer, and the southern and northern fires and the rest, together these five kinds of fires are, by traditional usage, the five classes. Besides this view, explaining the same again:

मनुष्याः पितरो देवाः गंधर्वोरगराक्षसाः । गंधर्वाः पितरो देवा असुरा यक्षराक्षसाः ॥ (*manuṣyāḥ pitaro devāḥ gaṃdharvoragarākṣasāḥ | gaṃdharvāḥ pitaro devā asurā yakṣarākṣasāḥ ‖*)

(Bṛ. De. 7-68)

According to the first view the Uraga-Rākṣasas are one group; according to the second view the Yakṣa-Rākṣasas are another group. And, *(the sentence is cut by the end of the window as supplied and continues in the next window)*

### Printed p. 380
*Running head: 380 ಸಾಯಣಭಾಷ್ಯಸಹಿತಾ [ ಮಂ. ೧. ಆ. ೨೨. ಸೂ. ೧೬೪] (as supplied; "ಆ." for the Anuvāka as on p. 376).*

यास्कौपमन्यनावेतानाहतुः पंच वै जनान् । निषादपंचमान्वर्णान् मन्यते शाकटायनः ॥ (*yāskaupamanyanāvetānāhatuḥ paṃca vai janān | niṣādapaṃcamānvarṇān manyate śākaṭāyanaḥ ‖*)

(Bṛ. De. 7-69)

In this sentence the authors of the Bṛhaddevatā say that Yāska's view is the first one; but the author of the Nirukta has only stated the view of Aupamanyu and others, and has not stated his own view definitively. Probably he too may have accepted that view.

ऋत्विजो यजमानं च शाकपूणिस्तु मन्यते (*ṛtvijo yajamānaṃ ca śākapūṇistu manyate*) ।

(Bṛ. De. 7-10) *[as supplied: printed "ಬೃ ದೇ." without the full stop after the first word]*

Another opinion is stated: that, according to Śākapūṇi, the five groups are the four priests beginning with the Hotṛ, together with the sacrificer. Besides this:

चक्षुः श्रोत्रं मनो वाक् च प्राणश्चेत्यात्मवादिनः । गंधर्वाप्सरसो देवा मनुष्याः पितरस्तथा ॥ सर्वाश्च ब्राह्मणे चैव श्रूयंते हैतरेयके ॥ (*cakṣuḥ śrotraṃ mano vāk ca prāṇaścetyātmavādinaḥ | gaṃdharvāpsaraso devā manuṣyāḥ pitarastathā ‖ sarvāśca brāhmaṇe caiva śrūyaṃte haitareyake ‖*)

(Bṛ. De. 7-21)

The eye, the ear, the mind, speech and the breath: these five are the five peoples, according to the view of the teachers of the doctrine of the Self (adhyātma-vādins). That they are the Gandharvas and the rest is stated in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (Ai. Brā. 3-31). Such five peoples, says the explanation in the Bṛhaddevatā also, may enjoy the oblation, thus Agni gave his answer to the gods; and in it the differences of opinion are cited. Not only that: in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad and other texts also, it is described that the tenfold guardians of the worlds and the rest, as stated in the present Ṛk, are the cause of the activity of the world, and, being subject to this original principle, keep its command.

तस्मा उ ह दमस्ते वा एते पंचान्ये पंचान्ये दश संतः । (*tasmā u ha damaste vā ete paṃcānye paṃcānye daśa saṃtaḥ |*)

(Bhā. U. 4-3-8) *[as supplied: the abbreviation "ಭಾ. ಉ." is kept as printed]*

Here the first word पंच (*paṃca*) is understood as the wind, fire, sun, moon and water; the second पंच (*paṃca*) as breath, speech, eye, ear *[as supplied: printed ಶೋತ್ರ]* and mind. Further, just as Sāyaṇa explained पंचलोकपालाः (*paṃcalokapālāḥ*) in the present Ṛk, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad also:

ते ना एते पंच ब्रह्मपुरुषाः स्वर्गस्य लोकस्य द्वारपाः । (*te nā ete paṃca brahmapuruṣāḥ svargasya lokasya dvārapāḥ |*)

(Chā. U. 3-13-6)

### Printed p. 381
*Running head: [ಅ. ೨. ಅ. ೩. ಪ. ೧೬] ಮುಗ್ವೇದಸಂಹಿತಾ 381 (as supplied: "ಪ." for ವ., "ಮುಗ್ವೇದ" for ಋಗ್ವೇದ; the page splitter did not recognise this head and the script inserted the page mark).*

it is said that they are the five Brahma-puruṣas, the door-keepers of heaven. Thus, although in many places the matter described in "दश युक्ता वहंति (*daśa yuktā vahaṃti*)" is indicated, since in all these contexts the words दश (*daśa*) and पंच (*paṃca*) are interpreted in the way suited to the respective circumstances, the authors of the Nirukta and the others themselves hold that one definite meaning cannot be stated. In the present context, since the meaning as Sāyaṇa has explained it, पंच लोकपालाः इंद्रादयः, वर्णात्मकाः पंजजनाः (*paṃca lokapālāḥ iṃdrādayaḥ, varṇātmakāḥ paṃjajanāḥ*) *[as supplied: printed ಪಂಜಜನಾಃ]*, fits, to interpret it in another way would be improper. That is to say: all beings, gods and men and the rest, follow the command of this principle of the universe and carry on the affairs of the world. In this immortal wheel, rise and fall are natural. Although the original principle is undecaying, to all that depends on it manifestation and disappearance belong in the form of recurrence. The sage Bādhva says this very thing in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka:

महापुरुष इति यमवोचाम संवत्सर एव प्रध्वंसयन्नन्यानि भूतानैक्या भावयन्नन्यानि तस्यैतस्यासावादित्यो रसः । स यश्चायमशरीरः प्रज्ञात्मा यश्चासावादित्य एकमेतदिति विद्यात् । तस्मात्पुरुषं पुरुषं प्रत्यादित्यो भवति ॥ (*mahāpuruṣa iti yamavocāma saṃvatsara eva pradhvaṃsayannanyāni bhūtānaikyā bhāvayannanyāni tasyaitasyāsāvādityo rasaḥ | sa yaścāyamaśarīraḥ prajñātmā yaścāsāvāditya ekametaditi vidyāt | tasmātpuruṣaṃ puruṣaṃ pratyādityo bhavati ‖*)

(Ai. Ā. 3-2-3-7 to 9)

He whom we call the Mahāpuruṣa (great person) is of the form of the year. During the revolution of that year, rise and fall must befall all beings. The essence of this year is Āditya. The person who is bodiless and of the nature of consciousness (prajñātman) and this Āditya are one and not different. Therefore the portion of this Āditya pervades every individual soul and spreads the reflection of one single principle in all. Here, when the sage Bādhva states the identity of the Mahāpuruṣa, the year and Āditya, he, in order to show support for his view, has said:

चित्रं देवानामुदगादनीकं चक्षुर्मित्रस्य वरुणस्याग्नेः । आप्रा द्यावापृथिवी अंतरिक्षं सूर‍्य आत्मा जगतस्तस्थुषश्च ॥ (*citraṃ devānāmudagādanīkaṃ cakṣurmitrasya varuṇasyāgneḥ | āprā dyāvāpṛthivī aṃtarikṣaṃ sūrya ātmā jagatastasthuṣaśca ‖*)

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-115-1)

The Āditya, who is of the form of the eye for Mitra, Varuṇa and Agni, has risen. He has pervaded fully the earth, the atmosphere and the heavenly world. Āditya is the inner Self of the moving world and of the stationary world, and he pervades the world.

सूर्यस्य चक्षुः रजसा आवृतं एति (*sūryasya cakṣuḥ rajasā āvṛtaṃ eti*)—here the word रजस् (*rajas*) is interpreted as water. Showing also the other meanings that this word has, the author of the Nirukta says,

### Printed p. 382
*Running head: 382 ಸಾಯಣಭಾಷ್ಯಸಹಿತಾ [ ಮಂ. ೧. ಅ. ೨೨. ಸೂ. ೧೬೪.] (as supplied).*

रजो रजतेज्योती रज उच्यते । उदकं रज उच्यते । लोका रजांस्युच्यंते । अस्यगहनी उच्यते ॥ (*rajo rajatejyotī raja ucyate | udakaṃ raja ucyate | lokā rajāṃsyucyaṃte | asyagahanī ucyate ‖*) *[as supplied: अस्यगहनी (*asyagahanī*) as printed]*

(Ni. 4-19)

Derived from the root रंज् (*raṃj*), which gives the meaning "to shine", the word रजस् (*rajas*) means light, water and the worlds. Having explained that it is also a synonym for blood (rakta) and ahas, it is stated that the author of the Nirukta has given examples from the Ṛk-saṃhitā to support these meanings; this was explained in the earlier part, that is, in the 11th part *[as supplied: "೧೧ನೇ ಭಾಗ"]* of the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, on page 58 *[as supplied: the figure "58" is in Latin digits]*.

Quoting the Ṛk

अज्जामुक्छैरहिं गृणीषे बुद्धे नदिनां रजःसु शीदन् । (*ajjāmukchairahiṃ gṛṇīṣe buddhe nadināṃ rajaḥsu śīdan |*)

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-34-16)

the author of the Nirukta says that in it the word रज (*raja*) means water; in the same way, in the present Ṛk also this word means water. रजसा आवृतं एति (*rajasā āvṛtaṃ eti*) is interpreted: the orb of the sun, covered with water, moves around the atmosphere.

अपाग्ं रसमुद्वयसग्ं सूरै संतग्ं समाहितमपाग्ं रसस्य यो रसस्तं वो गृह्णामुत्तमं। (*apāgṃ rasamudvayasagṃ sūrai saṃtagṃ samāhitamapāgṃ rasasya yo rasastaṃ vo gṛhṇāmuttamaṃ|*)

(Pa. Brā. *[as supplied: "ಪ. ಬ್ರಾ," with a comma]* 5-1-2-7)

The essence of the invigorating water is contained within the sun.

एता वा आपः स्वराजो यन्मरीचयस्ता यत्स्यंदंते । (*etā vā āpaḥ svarājo yanmarīcayastā yatsyaṃdaṃte |*)

(Śa. Brā. 5-3-4-21)

These rays of the sun, which are of the nature of streams, are the waters, and have unobstructed spreadings, and so on: thus the matter in which the orb of the sun, pervaded by water, is described, is described here. [This matter has been explained in detail under the Special Topics of the 12th Ṛk of this same sūkta, where the word पुरीषिणं (*purīṣiṇaṃ*) was explained.]

चक्षुः (*cakṣuḥ*)—चक्षुः ख्यातेर्वा चष्टेर्वा (*cakṣuḥ khyātervā caṣṭervā*). The author of the Nirukta has given the derivation of this word, saying that it is formed either from the root ख्या (*khyā*), which means knowledge, or from the root चक्षु (*cakṣu*), which means seeing (Ni. 4-3). Showing the basis for that, Sāyaṇa has given the meaning of this word: ज्ञानस्वभावं, सर्वस्य चक्षुःस्थानीयं वा (*jñānasvabhāvaṃ, sarvasya cakṣuḥsthānīyaṃ vā*) *[as supplied: the bhāṣya on p. 376 reads khyāna- for jñāna-]*, that is, either the orb of the sun *[as supplied: printed ಸೂರಮಂಡಲ]*, which is of the nature of knowledge, or the orb of Āditya, which is of the form of the eye of the world.

सूर्यो यथा सर्वलोकस्य चक्षुः (*sūryo yathā sarvalokasya cakṣuḥ*) ।

(Kaṭha. 5-11)

As described in sentences such as this, it is described in the present Ṛk also. The idea is that in this orb of Āditya विश्वा भुवनानि अर्पिता (*viśvā bhuvanāni arpitā*) (all the worlds are deposited).

*Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā (grammatical derivation)*

सनेमि (*sanemi*)—समाना नेमिः यस्य तत् सनेमि (*samānā nemiḥ yasya tat sanemi*). By समानस्य छंदसि (*samānasya chaṃdasi*)—(Pā. Sū. 6-3-84), substitution sa for the word samāna. The accent of the prakṛti of the former member comes.

अजरम् (*ajaram*)—न विद्यते जरा यस्य तत् (*na vidyate jarā yasya tat*); by नञ्खोजर (*nañkhojara*)—(Pā. Sū. 6-2-116) the latter member takes the ādyudātta accent.

ववृते (*vavṛte*)—the root वृतु वर्तने (*vṛtu vartane*). In the Vedic manner, लिट् (*liṭ*). A form ending in the third person singular *[as supplied: the Kannada word is printed "ಏಕಚನ" for ಏಕವಚನ]*. The tiṅanta-nighāta accent comes.

युक्ताः (*yuktāḥ*)—the root युजिर् योगे (*yujir yoge*). By निष्ठा (*niṣṭhā*) the suffix kta. By चोःकुः (*coḥkuḥ*) kutva. By the sūtra खरिच (*kharica*) cattva. By the pratyaya-accent it becomes antodātta.

चक्षुः (*cakṣuḥ*)—the root चक्षिज् व्यक्तायां वाचि (*cakṣij vyaktāyāṃ vāci*). By चक्षेः शिच्च (*cakṣeḥ śicca*) (Uṇ. Sū. 2-276 *[as supplied: printed ಉ- ಸೂ: ೨-೨೭೬]*) the suffix usi. It becomes śit. Since śitva is prescribed, the khyā substitution does not come. Because नित् (*nit*) continues by anuvṛtti, the ādyudātta accent comes. चक्षते रूपादिकमिति चक्षुः (*cakṣate rūpādikamiti cakṣuḥ*).

आवृतम् (*āvṛtam*)—the root वृञ् वरणे (*vṛñ varaṇe*). In the passive, the suffix kta. By गतिरनंतरः (*gatiranaṃtaraḥ*) (Pā. Sū. 6-2-49) the accent of the prakṛti for the gati (āṅ) comes. (End of Ṛk 14; printed ‖ 14 ‖.)
