**प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)**
सयुजा (*sayujā*)—those that are joined together; सखाया (*sakhāyā*)—those that appear as one form; द्वा सुपर्णा (*dvā suparṇā*)—two birds of excellent flight; समानं वृक्षं (*samānaṃ vṛkṣaṃ*)—the one and the same tree; परि षस्वजाते (*pari ṣasvajāte*)—have embraced (taken refuge in); तयोः (*tayoḥ*)—of those two; अन्यः (*anyaḥ*)—one; स्वादु (*svādu*)—sweet; पिप्पलं (*pippalaṃ*)—the fruit called pippala; अत्ति (*atti*)—eats; अन्यः (*anyaḥ*)—the other; अनश्नन् (*anaśnan*)—not eating; अभि चाकशीति (*abhi cākaśīti*)—looks on.

### Printed p. 413
*Running head: ಆ. ೨. ಅ. ೩ ವ. ೧೭ ] ಮುಗ್ವೇದಸಂಹಿತಾ 413 (as supplied; the script inserted this page marker because the head was not recognised).*

**भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)**
Two birds that are joined together, that appear as one form, and that are of excellent flight have taken refuge in one and the same tree. Of the two, one eats the sweet fruit. The other does not eat, but looks on.

**Printed English**
Two birds associated together, and mutual friends, take refuge in the same tree : one of them eats the sweet fig ; the other, abstaining from food. [sic] merely looks on

**विशेषविषयगळु (Viśeṣaviṣayagaḷu)**
Here, through the likeness of a pair of worldly birds, the individual self and the Supreme Self are praised. The meaning is: just as, in the world, two birds of excellent flight, appearing in one form, take refuge in one tree, so the individual self and the Supreme Self dwell in one body. But when it is said that of those two birds one eats a sweet fruit and the other merely sits looking on as a witness, the individual self is likened to the bird that enjoys the fruit, and the Supreme Self to the bird that sits as a mere witness without contact with the fruit.
सुपर्णा (*suparṇā*)—सुपतना ; शोभनगमनौ (*supatanā ; śobhanagamanau*). Because they fly well, these are suparṇas (good-winged). It may be said that for the individual self there is going through saṃsāra (worldly passage), for the Lord pure going.
सयुजा (*sayujā*)—समानयोगौ ; सहैव सर्वदा युक्तौ (*samānayogau ; sahaiva sarvadā yuktau*). Always joined together, united.
सखाया (*sakhāyā*)—समानख्यान् (*samānakhyān*) (sic, as supplied). The meaning is: those that show themselves in one and the same way. Having explained thus, Sāyaṇa then states the special meaning of the word सयुजा (*sayujā*) once more:
सयुजा-समानयोगौ । योगो नाम संबंधः । स च तादात्मलक्षणः, स एवात्मा जीवात्मनः स्वरूपं यस्य परमात्मनं स तदात्मा! (*sayujā-samānayogau | yogo nāma saṃbaṃdhaḥ | sa ca tādātmalakṣaṇaḥ, sa evātmā jīvātmanaḥ svarūpaṃ yasya paramātmanaṃ sa tadātmā!*) Yoga means relation. But there are many kinds of relation; here "equal yoga" means the relation of identity (tādātmya). The meaning is that the Supreme Self is of the very nature of the individual self and not different. By this qualifier the view of Bhāskara is refuted. How? According to that view there is difference between the individual self and the Supreme Self; that is an extreme doctrine, and such a doctrine of difference does not describe the true principle. Therefore, in order to refute it, the qualifier सयुजा (*sayujā*) is stated here.

### Printed p. 414
*Running head: 414 ಸಾಯುಣಭಾಷ್ಯಸಹಿತಾ [ ಮಂ. ೧. ಅ. ೨೨. ಸೂ. ೧೬೪] (as supplied; the script inserted this page marker because the head was not recognised).*

Sāyaṇa points out that there is room here for yet another objection, and gives the following answer to it as well:
ननु संबंधो द्विष्ठः स च पक्षिणोरिव भेदमपेक्षते अतः कथं ऐकात्म्यमिति। न । औपाधिकभेदं वास्तवाभेदं च अपेक्ष्य प्रवृत्तः । (*nanu saṃbaṃdho dviṣṭhaḥ sa ca pakṣiṇoriva bhedamapekṣate ataḥ kathaṃ aikātmyamiti| na | aupādhikabhedaṃ vāstavābhedaṃ ca apekṣya pravṛttaḥ |*)
It is clear that a relation belongs to two different things. If an objection is raised that it must be a relation like that of two different birds, and that where there is one thing alone there is no room for the description "yoga" or "relation", that is wrong. For difference is of two kinds: one is difference through a limiting adjunct (aupādhika), the other is real difference (vāstava). What is here is only the difference through an adjunct; there is no real difference here.
Or: ननु एकस्य यादृशं स्थानं तादृशमेव अन्यस्य इति व्युत्पत्ता भेदं स्पुटं प्रतिभाति कथं तादात्ममुच्यते इति न वक्तव्यं । (*nanu ekasya yādṛśaṃ sthānaṃ tādṛśameva anyasya iti vyutpattā bhedaṃ spuṭaṃ pratibhāti kathaṃ tādātmamucyate iti na vaktavyaṃ |*) When it is said that whatever place there is for one bird (the individual self), the same place there is for the other bird (the Supreme Self), does it not come to this, that this is one thing and that another? That too is not right. For here: नात्र परस्परं दृष्टांतदार्ष्टांतिकभावः । (*nātra parasparaṃ dṛṣṭāṃtadārṣṭāṃtikabhāvaḥ |*) Here no relation of illustration and thing illustrated, nor of the likened and that to which it is likened, has been stated between the two, one saying "like this, that". This intention is made clear by the qualifier सखायौ (*sakhāyau*) (sic, as supplied; the Ṛk has सखाया (*sakhāyā*)). यस्य यादृशं ज्ञानं परमात्मनः तदेव ज्ञानं इतरस्यापि जीवा त्मनः, तदेव ज्ञानमितरस्यापि जीवात्मनः इति सखायौ इत्युच्यते । (*yasya yādṛśaṃ jñānaṃ paramātmanaḥ tadeva jñānaṃ itarasyāpi jīvā tmanaḥ, tadeva jñānamitarasyāpi jīvātmanaḥ iti sakhāyau ityucyate |*) *[as supplied: the clause "tadeva jñānam itarasyāpi jīvātmanaḥ" is printed twice in this passage, the first time with a line-break inside "jīvā-tmanaḥ".]* The answer is given that the qualifier सखायौ (*sakhāyau*) is there to show that whatever light and appearance the Supreme Self has, the same light and appearance the individual self has also. Therefore the identity (aikātmya) is established here. By this, real difference also is refuted. Śaṅkarācārya, explaining this in his commentary on the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad, says:
सयुजा सयुज् सहैव सर्वदा युक्तौ, सखाया सखायौ समानख्यान् समानाभिव्यक्ति कारणावेवंभूत् संतः । (*sayujā sayuj sahaiva sarvadā yuktau, sakhāyā sakhāyau samānakhyān samānābhivyakti kāraṇāvevaṃbhūt saṃtaḥ |*)
(P. U. Śaṃ. Bhā. 3-1-1) *[as supplied: the abbreviation reads "ಪ. ಉ. ಶಂ. ಭಾ"; kept as printed.]*
The meaning is: having equal fame (khyāti); having one cause that makes them shine and appear.
वृक्षो व्रश्चनात् । वृत्वा क्षां तिष्ठतीति वा । क्षा क्षियतेर्निवासकर्मणः । (*vṛkṣo vraścanāt | vṛtvā kṣāṃ tiṣṭhatīti vā | kṣā kṣiyaternivāsakarmaṇaḥ |*) It is derived from the root व्रश् (*vraś*), which gives the meaning "to be cut down"; or else the name is well known because it gives the sense of covering the earth, which is the place of dwelling, and standing on it. (Ni. 2-6.) Where it is said that in the Ṛk at hand both rest on one and the same tree,

### Printed p. 415
*Running head: ಅ. ೨. ಅ. ೩. ಪ. ೧೭ ]  ಪುಗ್ವೇದಸಂಹಿತಾ  415 (as supplied; the script inserted this page marker because the head was not recognised).*

एकं वृक्षं वृक्षमिवोच्छेदनसामान्याच्छरीरं वृक्षं परिषस्वजाते परिष्वक्तवंतौ। (*ekaṃ vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣamivocchedanasāmānyāccharīraṃ vṛkṣaṃ pariṣasvajāte pariṣvaktavaṃtau|*)
(Mu. U. Śaṃ. Bhā. 3-1-1)
"Equal" means: they have embraced the tree that is one, with no special mark, a support for knowing. Here, because of the likeness of being destroyed like a tree, the body is likened to a tree. This perishable tree is described in Śaṅkara's commentary as follows:
अयं हि वृक्षः ऊर्ध्वमूलोऽवाक्याखोऽश्वत्थोऽव्यक्तमूलप्रभवः क्षेत्रसंज्ञकः सर्वप्राणिकर्मफलाश्रयः । (*ayaṃ hi vṛkṣaḥ ūrdhvamūlo 'vākyākho 'śvattho 'vyaktamūlaprabhavaḥ kṣetrasaṃjñakaḥ sarvaprāṇikarmaphalāśrayaḥ |*)
(Mu. U. Śaṃ. Bhā. 3-1-1)
This tree is the aśvattha (peepal) with roots above and branches below. Born of the root called the unmanifest, named the field (kṣetra), it is the support of the fruit of the actions of all beings. And this same tree:
तं परिष्कृतवंतौ सुपर्णाविविनाद्याकामकर्मवासनाश्रयलिंगोपाध्यात्मेश्वरौ । तयोः परिष्कृतयोरन्य एकः क्षेत्रज्ञो लिंगोपाधिवृक्षमाश्रितः पिप्पलं कर्मनिष्पन्नं सुखदुःखलक्षणं फलं साद्वनेकविचित्रवेदनास्वादरूपं स्वाद्वत्ति भक्षयत्युपभुंक्तेविवेकतः ॥ (*taṃ pariṣkṛtavaṃtau suparṇāvivinādyākāmakarmavāsanāśrayaliṃgopādhyātmeśvarau | tayoḥ pariṣkṛtayoranya ekaḥ kṣetrajño liṃgopādhivṛkṣamāśritaḥ pippalaṃ karmaniṣpannaṃ sukhaduḥkhalakṣaṇaṃ phalaṃ sādvanekavicitravedanāsvādarūpaṃ svādvatti bhakṣayatyupabhuṃktevivekataḥ ‖*)
(Mu. U. Śaṃ. Dhā. 3-1-1) *[as supplied: the abbreviation reads "ಶಂ. ಧಾ" here; kept as printed.]*
The individual self and the Lord, who has the adjunct of the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra) that is the support of ignorance, desire and the impressions of action, have taken refuge like two birds. Of these two who have taken refuge, one, namely the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) with the subtle-body adjunct, resting on the tree, eats the pippala, the sweet fruit; that is, he enjoys the fruit, born of his own action, of the nature of pleasure and pain, the savour of many and various feelings.
अनश्नन्नन्य इतर ईश्वरो नित्यशुद्धबुद्धमुक्तस्वभावः सर्वज्ञः सर्वसत्त्वोपाधिरीश्वरो नाश्नाति ॥ (*anaśnannanya itara īśvaro nityaśuddhabuddhamuktasvabhāvaḥ sarvajñaḥ sarvasattvopādhirīśvaro nāśnāti ‖*)
(Mu. U. Śaṃ. Bhā. 3-1-1) *[as supplied: the reference is printed "ಮ:೦. ಉ ಶಂ. ಭಾ. ೩-೧-೧", garbled; kept as printed.]*
The other does not eat; being the Lord, of ever pure, awakened and free nature, omniscient, the adjunct of all sattva, he does not eat. While this is so described, Sāyaṇa, anticipating yet another objection, has given an answer to it as well:
न च जीवस्य वस्तुतः ईश्वरत्वे कथं जीवबुद्ध्या संसारशोक् इति वाच्यं तयोर्मोहकृतत्वात् ॥ (*na ca jīvasya vastutaḥ īśvaratve kathaṃ jīvabuddhyā saṃsāraśok iti vācyaṃ tayormohakṛtatvāt ‖*)

### Printed p. 416
*Running head: 416 ಸಾಯಣಭಾಷ್ಯಸಹಿತಾ [ ಮಂ. ೧. ಅ. ೨೨. ಸೂ.೧೬೪] (as supplied).*

"If the individual self really is the Lord, how can there be the sorrow of saṃsāra through the notion of being an individual?" There is no room for this question, because saṃsāra and sorrow are caused by delusion. Having shown that this objection is easily removed, he supports his argument by quoting a sentence of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad:
समाने वृक्षे पुरुषो निमग्नोऽनीशया शोचति मुह्यमानः । जुष्टं यदा पश्यत्यन्यमीशमस्य महिमानमिति वीतशोकः ॥ (*samāne vṛkṣe puruṣo nimagno 'nīśayā śocati muhyamānaḥ | juṣṭaṃ yadā paśyatyanyamīśamasya mahimānamiti vītaśokaḥ ‖*)
(Mu. U. 3-1-2)
"On the same tree the person, sunk in it, grieves, deluded by helplessness" is the idea; this he explains with the words एक एव शरीरे पूर्णः पुरुषः (*eka eva śarīre pūrṇaḥ puruṣaḥ*) .... .... .... and so on (ellipsis as printed). Its meaning is as follows.
On one tree, that is, in the body spoken of above, the person, that is the individual self who is the enjoyer, carrying the burden of ignorance, desire, action, hope of fruit and so on, sunk like a gourd-float in the water of the sea (*alābur iva sāmudre jale nimagnaḥ*—Śaṅkara's commentary), and possessed of the notion that he is the body, obtains experiences such as "I am the doer, I am happy, I am unhappy", in the forms of birth, death and the rest.
यदा तु जुष्टं नित्यतृप्तमन्यं संसारशोकातीतं परमेश्वरं पश्यति (*yadā tu juṣṭaṃ nityatṛptamanyaṃ saṃsāraśokātītaṃ parameśvaraṃ paśyati*) .... .... ....
तदा वीतशोको देहाद्यतिरिक्तः (*tadā vītaśoko dehādyatiriktaḥ*) . . .... .... .... अस्य परमेश्वरस्य महिमानं प्राप्नोति (*asya parameśvarasya mahimānaṃ prāpnoti*)।
When he realises the Lord, who is beyond the sorrow of saṃsāra, then, free from sorrow and released from the fetters of the body and the rest, he obtains the very greatness of the Lord. The meaning is that as soon as that conception arises, he obtains the very form of the Lord.
तस्माद्वस्तुतः एक एव । भेदस्तु मोहकृत इति सिद्धं । (*tasmādvastutaḥ eka eva | bhedastu mohakṛta iti siddhaṃ |*) Therefore the principle that is in truth one appears, because of the veil of delusion, as having difference; this is the established point.
अनश्नन्नन्यो अभिचाकशीति (*anaśnannanyo abhicākaśīti*)—अन्यः परमात्मा तु आप्तकामत्वेन स्पृहाया अभ वात् अभुंजानः । (*anyaḥ paramātmā tu āptakāmatvena spṛhāyā abha vāt abhuṃjānaḥ |*) Because the Lord is of fulfilled desire, he does not eat but simply goes on looking. *[as supplied: "ಅಭ" and "ವಾತ್" are split by a line-break in the print.]*
आप्तकामस्य का स्पृहा । (*āptakāmasya kā spṛhā |*)
(Mā. U. Kā. 1-9) *[as supplied: the reference is printed "ಮಾ ಉ. ಕಾ. ೧-೯"; kept as printed.]*
Thus the fulfilled-desire nature of the Lord is described; the same point is explained in the Ṛk at hand. The same Ṛk is explained in the Nirukta as follows—

*Grammar (transcribed, not explained):*

सस्वजाते (*sasvajāte*) *[as supplied: so printed, without the prefix pari]*—root ष्वंज परिष्वंगे (*ṣvaṃja pariṣvaṃge*); Vedic liṭ, third person dual, ending ātām; टित आत्मनेपदानां (*ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ*) (Pā. #### Ṛk 21
**॥ संहितापाठः ॥**
> यत्रा॑ सुप॒र्णा अ॒मृत॑स्य भा॒गमनि॑मेषं वि॒दथा॑भि॒स्वरं॑ति ।
> इ॒नो विश्व॑स्य॒ भुव॑नस्य गो॒पाः स मा॒ धीरः॒ पाक॒मत्रा॑
> विवेश ॥ २१ ॥
*[as supplied: the label "ಕನ್ನಡ" printed after the Saṃhitā block, normalised by the script to Pada-pāṭha.]*
**॥ पदपाठः ॥**
> यत्र । सुपर्णाः । अमृतस्य । भागं । अनिमेषं । विदथा । अभिस्वरंति ।
> इनः । विश्वस्य । भुवनस्य । गोपाः । सः । मा । धीरः । पाकं । अत्र । आ । विवेश ॥ २१ ॥
*[as supplied: the label "ಸಹಾಯಧರ್ಮ" printed after the Pada block, normalised by the script to Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya.]*
**॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥**
> यत्रादित्यमंडले सुपर्णाः सुपतनाः शोभनगमना रश्मयोऽमृतस्योदकस्य
> भागं भजनीयमंशमादायानिमेषमनवरतं विदथा वेदनेन ज्ञानेनास्माभिरेवं
> कर्तव्यमिति बुद्ध्याभिस्वरंति अभिप्रावयंति । यश्च विश्वस्य भुवनस्य भूतजातस्येनः
> स्वामी तथा तस्यै व गोपा गोपायिता रक्षिता। आयमादित्यः स परमेश्वरो धीरो
> धीमान् प्राण्यनुग्रहबुद्धियुक्त सन् मा मां पाकं पक्तव्यमपक्वप्रज्ञमत्रास्मिन्स्वकीयमंडल आ विवेश । प्रवेशयति । अत्रास्मदीये देहे ना नियामकतया
> प्रविष्ट इत्यधिदैवतपक्षे ॥ अढाध्यात्मपक्षे ॥ यत्र यस्मिन्नात्मनि सुपर्णाः शोभनपतनानि स्वस्वविषयग्रहणाय गमनकुशलानींद्रियाणि चक्षुरादीन्यमृतस्य भागं ।
> अत्र विषयावच्चिन्नचैतन्यममृतमित्युच्यते । तस्य भागं भजनीयं स्वस्वांशमनिमेषं
> निमेषरहितमनारतं विदथा वेदनेन वृत्त्यवच्छिन्नचैतन्यॆनावरुद्धान्यभिस्वरंति अभिप्रयंति आवरणापगमनेन स्फोरयंति । किंच यस्त्विनः स्वाम्यस्य देहस्य विश्वस्य
> भुवनस्य गोपा गोपायिता रक्षिता । यद्वा । विश्वस्य भुवनस्य भूतजातस्य स्वाम्यस्य
> देहस्य गोपाः । अनेन तत्त्वपदार्थयोरेकत्वं प्रतिपादितं भवति । स परमेश्वरो
> धीरः समाधिनिष्ठः सर्वदाविक्रियो मा मां पाकं परिपक्वमनस्कं यागदानादिनापगतरजस्तमस्कत्वेन दर्पणवदतिनिर्मलसत्तोद्रिक्तमनस्कं मामा विवेश । उक्तरूपे
> चित्ते तादृशं वस्तु स्पुरतीत्यर्थः । यद्वा । अपरिपक्वमना अहं पूर्वमज्ञानदशायां मदन्य ईश्वरोऽस्तीत्यविद्वान् ततः परमस्ति कश्चित्सर्वज्ञः सर्वेश्वरः सत्यज्ञानादिलक्षण इति निश्चित्य पश्चाद्गुरुशास्त्राभ्यां स एवाहमस्मीति मत्ता एवं पारंपर्ये-

> *yatrādityamaṃḍale suparṇāḥ supatanāḥ śobhanagamanā raśmayo 'mṛtasyodakasya*
> *bhāgaṃ bhajanīyamaṃśamādāyānimeṣamanavarataṃ vidathā vedanena jñānenāsmābhirevaṃ*
> *kartavyamiti buddhyābhisvaraṃti abhiprāvayaṃti | yaśca viśvasya bhuvanasya bhūtajātasyenaḥ*
> *svāmī tathā tasyai va gopā gopāyitā rakṣitā| āyamādityaḥ sa parameśvaro dhīro*
> *dhīmān prāṇyanugrahabuddhiyukta san mā māṃ pākaṃ paktavyamapakvaprajñamatrāsminsvakīyamaṃḍala ā viveśa | praveśayati | atrāsmadīye dehe nā niyāmakatayā*
> *praviṣṭa ityadhidaivatapakṣe ‖ aḍhādhyātmapakṣe ‖ yatra yasminnātmani suparṇāḥ śobhanapatanāni svasvaviṣayagrahaṇāya gamanakuśalānīṃdriyāṇi cakṣurādīnyamṛtasya bhāgaṃ |*
> *atra viṣayāvaccinnacaitanyamamṛtamityucyate | tasya bhāgaṃ bhajanīyaṃ svasvāṃśamanimeṣaṃ*
> *nimeṣarahitamanārataṃ vidathā vedanena vṛttyavacchinnacaitanyènāvaruddhānyabhisvaraṃti abhiprayaṃti āvaraṇāpagamanena sphorayaṃti | kiṃca yastvinaḥ svāmyasya dehasya viśvasya*
> *bhuvanasya gopā gopāyitā rakṣitā | yadvā | viśvasya bhuvanasya bhūtajātasya svāmyasya*
> *dehasya gopāḥ | anena tattvapadārthayorekatvaṃ pratipāditaṃ bhavati | sa parameśvaro*
> *dhīraḥ samādhiniṣṭhaḥ sarvadāvikriyo mā māṃ pākaṃ paripakvamanaskaṃ yāgadānādināpagatarajastamaskatvena darpaṇavadatinirmalasattodriktamanaskaṃ māmā viveśa | uktarūpe*
> *citte tādṛśaṃ vastu spuratītyarthaḥ | yadvā | aparipakvamanā ahaṃ pūrvamajñānadaśāyāṃ madanya īśvaro 'stītyavidvān tataḥ paramasti kaścitsarvajñaḥ sarveśvaraḥ satyajñānādilakṣaṇa iti niścitya paścādguruśāstrābhyāṃ sa evāhamasmīti mattā evaṃ pāraṃparye-*

### Printed p. 419
*Running head: ಅ. ೨. ಚ. ೩. ವ. ೧೬.] ಋಗ್ವೇದಸಂಹಿತಾ 419 (as supplied).*

*[Continuing the Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya of Ṛk 21.]*
> णावगत्यासंभावनाविपरीतभावने व्युदस्य भावनया साक्षात्कृत्य परिपूर्णः परमात्माभूवमित्यर्थः । अयमेव स मा धीरः पाकमत्रा विवेशेत्यनेनोच्यते । नन्ननवच्छिन्नस्य परमात्मनः सर्वत्रव्याप्तत्वात्पाप्तिरेव नोपपद्यते संप्रत्यत्र प्राप्तिर्द्विविधा
> प्राप्तप्राप्तिरप्राप्तप्राप्तिश्चेति । प्राप्तस्यापि कंठे चामीकरन्यायेनावरणाज्ञानहानद्वारेण प्राप्तिरुपपद्यते । अस्यमंत्रस्य यन्नि रुक्तं यत्र सुपर्णाः सुपतना आदित्यरश्मय इत्यादिकं तदत्र द्रष्टव्यं । नि. ३-१२ ॥
*Gist:* In the sun's orb the rays draw water and the Lord of all protects; read as the Supreme Self, he enters the immature seeker and dissolves his ignorance (two readings).

**प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)**
यत्र (*yatra*)—in which orb of the sun; सुपर्णाः (*suparṇāḥ*)—rays of excellent spread; विदथा (*vidathā*)—by their knowledge of their duty; अमृतस्य (*amṛtasya*)—of the water; अंशं (*aṃśaṃ*) *[as supplied: the Ṛk has भागं (*bhāgaṃ*)]*—the portion; अनिमेषं (*animeṣaṃ*)—always; अभिस्वरंति (*abhisvaraṃti*)—make to flow; (and) (यः (*yaḥ*)—who); विश्वस्य (*viśvasya*)—of all; भुवनस्य (*bhuvanasya*)—of the world; इनः (*inaḥ*)—lord (and likewise); गोपाः (*gopāḥ*)—protector; सः (*saḥ*)—that Supreme Lord in the form of the sun; धीरः (*dhīraḥ*)—having a mind of grace; मानन्नन्नु (*mānannannu*) *[as supplied: so printed, for "mām" and "me"]*—me; पाकं (*pākaṃ*)—though endowed with an immature intellect; अत्र (*atra*)—in this his orb; आ विवेश (*ā viveśa*)—causes to enter.

**भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)**
In which orb of the sun the rays of excellent spread, by their knowledge of their duty, always cause a portion of water to flow, and who is lord and protector of the whole world, that Supreme Lord in the form of the sun, having a mind of grace, causes even me, though I am of immature knowledge, to enter into this his orb.

**Printed English**
Where the smooth-gliding (rays), cognizant (of their duty), distil the prepetual [sic] portion of ambrosial (water); there has the lord ,and [sic] steadfast protector of all beings consigned me, (though) immature (in wisdom).

**विशेषविषयगळु (Viśeṣaviṣayagaḷu)**
The Nirukta's explanation of this Ṛk is twofold. First:
यत्र सुपर्णाः सुपतना आदित्यरश्मयः अमृतस्य भागं उदकस्य अनिमिषंतो वेदनेनाभिस्वरंतीति वाभिप्रयंतीति वा । ईश्वरः सर्वेषां भूतानां गोपायितादित्यः । ' स मा धीरः पाकमत्राविवेश ' । धीरो धीमान् (*yatra suparṇāḥ supatanā ādityaraśmayaḥ amṛtasya bhāgaṃ udakasya animiṣaṃto vedanenābhisvaraṃtīti vābhiprayaṃtīti vā | īśvaraḥ sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ gopāyitādityaḥ | ' sa mā dhīraḥ pākamatrāviveśa ' | dhīro dhīmān*)

### Printed p. 420
*Running head: 420 ಸಾಯಣಭಾವ್ಯಸಹಿತಾ [ ಮಂ. ೧. ಅ. ೨೨. ಸೂ. ೧೬೪] (as supplied; "bhāvya" for "bhāṣya"; the script inserted this page marker because the head was not recognised).*

पाकः पक्तव्यो भवति “ विपक्षप्रज्ञ आदित्यः ” इत्युपनिषद्वर्णो भवतीत्यधिदैवतं । (*pākaḥ paktavyo bhavati “ vipakṣaprajña ādityaḥ ” ityupaniṣadvarṇo bhavatītyadhidaivataṃ |*)
*[stray line as supplied: ( ൨. ൨-൧ )]*
The sun's rays of very attractive flight, with full knowledge, spreading toward the water, perform their duties in that sun, who is the protector of the entire world and of fully ripened understanding; that sun has approached me, of unripe knowledge, with a mind of grace. This is the explanation relating to the divinity (adhidaivata).
The second reading:
अथाध्यात्मं । यत्र सुपर्णाः सुपतनानींद्रियाण्यमृतस्य भागं ज्ञानस्यानिवि:- षंतो वेदनेनाभिस्वरंतीति वाभिप्रयंतीति वा । ईश्वरः सर्वेषामिंद्रियाणां गोपायितात्मा स मा धीरः पाकमत्राविवेशेति धीरो धीमान् पाकः पक्तव्यो भवति विपक्वप्रज्ञ आत्मेत्यात्मगतिमाचष्टे ॥ (*athādhyātmaṃ | yatra suparṇāḥ supatanānīṃdriyāṇyamṛtasya bhāgaṃ jñānasyānivi:- ṣaṃto vedanenābhisvaraṃtīti vābhiprayaṃtīti vā | īśvaraḥ sarveṣāmiṃdriyāṇāṃ gopāyitātmā sa mā dhīraḥ pākamatrāviveśeti dhīro dhīmān pākaḥ paktavyo bhavati vipakvaprajña ātmetyātmagatimācaṣṭe ‖*) *[as supplied: the line-end hyphen in "anivi-ṣanto" is printed ":-".]*
(Ni. 3-12)
The spiritual (ādhyātma) explanation is as follows. In which body the senses, that spread easily (towards the objects that attract them), knowing their own nature, move toward knowledge, the means of immortality, in that body the self (the Supreme Self), lord of all the senses and of full understanding, has approached me, of unripe knowledge, with a mind of grace. Having explained it in these two ways, he then gives incidentally the etymology of the words suparṇa and dhīra.
धीरो धीमान् । (*dhīro dhīmān |*) The meaning is: one who has understanding. This word is read among the names of the intelligent. (Ni. 3-9.) In present usage the word dhīra comes to mean "courageous". In the Vedas and the Upaniṣads too this word is used in the sense of "wise, discriminating"; there too, since the dhīra is wise, and has such qualities as conquering fear and being fearless and of tranquil mind even in time of calamity, the sense of "courageous" is also implied.
युवा सुवासाः परिवीत आगात्स उ श्रेयान्भवति जायमानः । तं धीरासः कवयः उन्नयंति स्वाध्यो३ मनसा देवयंतः । (*yuvā suvāsāḥ parivīta āgātsa u śreyānbhavati jāyamānaḥ | taṃ dhīrāsaḥ kavayaḥ unnayaṃti svādhyo3 manasā devayaṃtaḥ |*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-8-4)
in such Ṛks, and
श्रेयश्च प्रेयश्च मनुष्यमेतस्त् संसरीत्य विविनक्ति धीरः । श्रेयो हि धीरोऽभिप्रेयसो वृणीते प्रियो मंदो योगक्षेमाद्वणीते ॥ (*śreyaśca preyaśca manuṣyametast saṃsarītya vivinakti dhīraḥ | śreyo hi dhīro 'bhipreyaso vṛṇīte priyo maṃdo yogakṣemādvaṇīte ‖*)
(Kaṭha. 2-2)

### Printed p. 421
*Running head: ಅ. ೨. ಅ. ೪ ವ ೧೭.] ಋಗ್ವೇದಸಂಹಿತಾ 421 (as supplied; the script had marked this page "422" and the true head of p. 422 is below, so the marker was repaired by hand).*

in such Upaniṣad sentences also the word dhīra has the meaning "wise, understanding".
सुपर्णाः (*suparṇāḥ*)—the word suparṇa, though read among the names of rays (Ni. 2-15) and among the names of horses (Ni. 2-27), is used also in the senses of bird, arrow and so on. Whatever meaning is given, it conveys the idea of "good flight", that is, "that which moves charmingly". For example,
वि सुपर्णो अंतरिक्षाण्यख्यद्दभीरवेपा असुरः सुनीथः । क्वेषिदानीं सूर्यः कश्चिकेत कतमां द्यां रश्मिरस्या ततान ॥ (*vi suparṇo aṃtarikṣāṇyakhyaddabhīravepā asuraḥ sunīthaḥ | kveṣidānīṃ sūryaḥ kaściketa katamāṃ dyāṃ raśmirasyā tatāna ‖*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-35-7)
in this Ṛk there is a description of the ray, of deep tremor, pervading the whole atmosphere and attracting the mind. The word suparṇa here refers to the ray. The words शोभनपतना रश्मयः (*śobhanapatanā raśmayaḥ*) show a special quality of the ray. Likewise,
इंद्रं मित्रं वरुणमग्निमाहुरथो दिव्यः स सुपर्णो गरुत्मान् । एकं सद्विप्रा बहुधा वदंत्यग्निं यमं मातरिश्वानमाहुः ॥ (*iṃdraṃ mitraṃ varuṇamagnimāhuratho divyaḥ sa suparṇo garutmān | ekaṃ sadviprā bahudhā vadaṃtyagniṃ yamaṃ mātariśvānamāhuḥ ‖*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-164-46)
in the 46th Ṛk of this same sūkta, सुपतनः गरुत्मान् (*supatanaḥ garutmān*) refers to a bird, Garuḍa, whose flight through the sky is attractive. And in the Ṛk explained before (164-20) too, the special quality of the worldly bird is said to be described. Likewise,
उक्षा समुद्रो अरुषः सुपर्णः पूर्वस्य योनिं पितुरा विवेश । मध्ये दिवो निहितः पृश्नरश्मा वि चक्रमे रजसस्पात्यंतौ ॥ (*ukṣā samudro aruṣaḥ suparṇaḥ pūrvasya yoniṃ piturā viveśa | madhye divo nihitaḥ pṛśnaraśmā vi cakrame rajasaspātyaṃtau ‖*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-47-3)
here it is explained as the sea (the atmosphere) of good motion, and in
सुपर्णं वस्ते मृगो अस्या दंतो गोभिः संनद्धा पतति प्रसूता । (*suparṇaṃ vaste mṛgo asyā daṃto gobhiḥ saṃnaddhā patati prasūtā |*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-75-11)
the Ṛk quoted in the Nirukta (Ni. 9-19), it is explained as an arrow of good flight. In the Ṛk at hand, on the side relating to the divinity it is explained as rays of good flight, and on the spiritual side as senses of good flight. When it is said सुपर्णा अभिस्वरंति (*suparṇā abhisvaraṃti*), what ideas are suggested on the side relating to the divinity and on the spiritual side must be examined.

### Printed p. 422
*Running head: 422 ಸಾಯುಧಭಾಷ್ಯಸಹಿತಾ । ಮಂ. ೧ ಆ. ೨೨. ಸೂ. ೧೬೦ (as supplied; "sūkta 160" is printed although the sūkta is 164; the script had not marked this page and it was inserted by hand).*

For the word अभिस्वरंति (*abhisvaraṃti*) the author of the Nirukta gives the meaning अभिप्रयंति (*abhiprayaṃti*). Durgācārya, explaining this, says (स्वशब्दोपतापयोः (*svaśabdopatāpayoḥ*)) that it is formed from the root स्वृ (*svṛ*) in the sense of heating, and the meaning is that they make all beings glow with heat; that is, by drawing the juice in the earth they make the earth glow with heat. This does not appear very agreeable. Therefore he shows another derivation of it too:
अथ अभिमुख्यन रसान् गृहीत्वा आदित्यमंडलं प्रयांति । (*atha abhimukhyana rasān gṛhītvā ādityamaṃḍalaṃ prayāṃti |*) The second meaning is stated: having drawn up the juice, they go toward the orb of the sun. In both of these meanings the drawing of juice is the main point; but in the first explanation it applies to heating the earth. Here, however, since the rays' readiness to protect the world is described, it is proper to say that, for the sake of performing that duty and by knowledge of the duty (विदथा (*vidathā*)), they take that juice to the sun and gather it there so as to favour the fall of rain. In the Ṛk-saṃhitā this word is used in two meanings. First,
रथानां न ये १ राः सनाभयो जिगीवांसो न शूरा अभिद्यवः । वरेयवो न मर्या धृतपुषोऽभिस्वर्तारो अर्कं न सुष्टुभः ॥ (*rathānāṃ na ye 1 rāḥ sanābhayo jigīvāṃso na śūrā abhidyavaḥ | vareyavo na maryā dhṛtapuṣo 'bhisvartāro arkaṃ na suṣṭubhaḥ ‖*) *[as supplied: "ಯೇ ೧ ರಾಃ" is printed with a numeral 1 inside the word.]*
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-78-4)
in this Ṛk the explanation अभिस्वर्तार अभितः शब्दयितारः । (*abhisvartāra abhitaḥ śabdayitāraḥ |*) is given, "those who recite words of praise"; so the word अभिस्वर (*abhisvara*) means praise-speech. Likewise,
नेमिं नमंति चक्षसा मेषं विप्रा अभिस्वरा । सुदीतयो वो अम्रहोऽपि कर्णॆ तरस्विनः समृक्वभिः ॥ (*nemiṃ namaṃti cakṣasā meṣaṃ viprā abhisvarā | sudītayo vo amraho 'pi karṇè tarasvinaḥ samṛkvabhiḥ ‖*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-97-12)
here too अभिस्वरा अभिस्वरणेन स्तोत्रेण । (*abhisvarā abhisvaraṇena stotreṇa |*) means "by a hymn of praise". Besides this it is used also in the sense of following one another.
एकपादभूयो द्विपदो वि चक्रमे द्विपात्रिपादमभ्येति पश्चात् । चतुष्पादेति द्विपदामभिस्वरे संपश्यन् पंक्तिरुपतिष्ठमानः ॥ (*ekapādabhūyo dvipado vi cakrame dvipātripādamabhyeti paścāt | catuṣpādeti dvipadāmabhisvare saṃpaśyan paṃktirupatiṣṭhamānaḥ ‖*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 18-17-8) *[as supplied: the reference is printed "೧೮-೧೭-೮"; kept as printed.]*
in this Ṛk, to explain that the superior and the inferior stand in mutual dependence and mutual following, it is described as अभिस्वरे संपश्यन् (*abhisvare saṃpaśyan*). Here the word अभिस्वर (*abhisvara*) means going toward: it means "go to meet" or "go following". In the Ṛk at hand it can apply in both these meanings. How? *[The Special Topics are cut by the end of the window as supplied, at "ಹೇಗೆಂದರೆ,", and continue in the next window.]*

### Printed p. 423
*Running head: ಆ. ೨. ರಾ. ೨. ವ. ೧೭ ] ಋಗ್ವೇದಸಂಹಿತಾ 423 (as supplied).*

*[Continuing the Special Topics of Ṛk 21 from the previous window.]*
शीर्ष्णः क्षीरं दुह्रते गावो अस्य वव्रिं वसाना उदकं पदापुः । (*śīrṣṇaḥ kṣīraṃ duhrate gāvo asya vavriṃ vasānā udakaṃ padāpuḥ |*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-164-7)
As described in this Ṛk, the one preceding this in the same sūkta, the rays of the sun, while performing the sun's duty, serve him both by pouring out water and by drawing the water up again and gathering it to Sūra *[as supplied: "ಸೂರನಲ್ಲಿಗೆ"]*. And knowing what is in his mind, they do their duties. Drawing water from the earth, going toward him, they again make things favourable to the fall of rain, and so on. As thus described, here too अमृतस्य भागं अभिस्वरंति (*amṛtasya bhāgaṃ abhisvaraṃti*) may mean that they take in a portion of the water (knowing their duty) and gather it to him; or it may mean that by their hymn, which is a form of their service, and by approaching him together with the water, they have urged him to pour down rain again.
अमृतस्य (*amṛtasya*)—on the side relating to the divinity, the word अमृत (*amṛta*) is explained as water. The author of the Nirukta has read this word among the names of water (Ni. 2-24), and when giving the explanation of this Ṛk also he explains it as उदकस्य (*udakasya*) (Ni. 3-12).
तस्य ये प्रांचो रश्मयः .... .... .... .... .... ता अमृता आप्तः । (*tasya ye prāṃco raśmayaḥ .... .... .... .... .... tā amṛtā āptaḥ |*) *[ellipsis ".... .... .... .... ...." as printed.]*
(Chā. U. 2-1-2)
In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, where the relation between the sun and the waters is told, the word अपः (*apaḥ*) has the qualifier अमृताः (*amṛtāḥ*). Śaṅkarācārya explains this as अमृतार्थत्वादत्यंतरसवत्य आपो भवंति (*amṛtārthatvādatyaṃtarasavatya āpo bhavaṃti*). Continuing this:
On the spiritual side: अमृतस्य ( अमरणधर्मणः ) ज्ञानस्य (*amṛtasya ( amaraṇadharmaṇaḥ ) jñānasya*)—as the author of the Nirukta explained, Sāyaṇa too has understood it, and he has also stated a qualification: explaining अत्र विषयावच्छिन्नचैतन्यं अमृतमित्र्युच्यते (*atra viṣayāvacchinnacaitanyaṃ amṛtamitryucyate*) *[as supplied: "ಮಿತ್ರ್ಯು" for the expected "ಮಿತ್ಯು"]*, he has shown the difference between consciousness limited by the object and consciousness limited by the mental modification. This explanation is like:
द्वे अक्षरे ब्रह्मपरे त्वनंते विद्याविद्ये निहिते यत्र गूढे । क्षरं त्वविद्या ह्यमृतं तु विद्या विद्याविद्ये ईशते यस्तु सोऽन्यः । (*dve akṣare brahmapare tvanaṃte vidyāvidye nihite yatra gūḍhe | kṣaraṃ tvavidyā hyamṛtaṃ tu vidyā vidyāvidye īśate yastu so 'nyaḥ |*)
(Prai. U. 5-8) *[as supplied: reference "ಪ್ರೈ. ಉ. ೫-೮"; kept as printed.]*
In the imperishable and endless Supreme Brahman, knowledge and ignorance are laid down. Of these, ignorance is perishable and knowledge is immortal; as this difference is shown, so here too the difference is shown between consciousness limited by the object and consciousness limited by the mental modification. The basis of both is the self alone. Therefore, with यत्र यस्मिन्नात्मनि अभिस्वरंति (*yatra yasminnātmani abhisvaraṃti*), the self, the one basis of both, is described.

### Printed p. 424
*Running head: 424 ಸಾಯಣಭಾಷ್ಯಸಹಿತಾ [ ಮಂ. ೧. ಆ. ೨೨. ಸೂ ೧೬೪] (as supplied).*

अनिमेषं (*animeṣaṃ*)—for this word the meaning in the sense of water is "unceasingly", and in the sense of knowledge "without a wink" (that which has no closing of the eyes).
धीरः पाकमत्रा विवेश (*dhīraḥ pākamatrā viveśa*)—Sāyaṇa has explained this in two ways. First:
स परमेश्वरः धीरः समाधिनिष्ठः सर्वदा अविक्रियो मां पाकं परि पक्वमनस्कं यागादिना अपगतरजस्तमस्कत्वेन दर्पणवदतिनिर्मलसत्तोद्रिक्तमनस्सं मां आ विवेश । (*sa parameśvaraḥ dhīraḥ samādhiniṣṭhaḥ sarvadā avikriyo māṃ pākaṃ pari pakvamanaskaṃ yāgādinā apagatarajastamaskatvena darpaṇavadatinirmalasattodriktamanassaṃ māṃ ā viveśa |*) *[as supplied: "ಪರಿ ಪಕ್ವ" is split by a line-break, and "ಮನಸ್ಸಂ" is printed where the bhāṣya of Ṛk 21 has "ಮನಸ್ಕಂ".]* The Supreme Lord, firm in samādhi, destroying through sacrifices and other good acts the qualities of rajas and tamas, entered me, who am fully ripened, filled with sattva, and as pure as a mirror. And secondly:
यद्वा, अपरिपक्वमनाः अहं पूर्वं अज्ञानदशायां मदन्यः ईश्वरोऽस्तीति अविद्वान् ततः परमस्ति कश्चित्सर्वज्ञः .... .... .... पश्चाद्गुरुशास्त्राभ्यां स एवाहमस्मीति मत्वा .... .... परिपूर्णः परमात्माभवं । (*yadvā, aparipakvamanāḥ ahaṃ pūrvaṃ ajñānadaśāyāṃ madanyaḥ īśvaro 'stīti avidvān tataḥ paramasti kaścitsarvajñaḥ .... .... .... paścādguruśāstrābhyāṃ sa evāhamasmīti matvā .... .... paripūrṇaḥ paramātmābhavaṃ |*) *[ellipses ".... .... ...." as printed.]* He has also explained: in the earlier state of the practice of knowledge, holding the notion of difference, "I am one, the Lord is another", and afterwards, through the study of the scriptures and the teaching of the teachers, giving up the notion of difference, I attained oneness with the Lord by the thought अहमस्मि (*ahamasmi*) ("I am"): this is the meaning. How the word पाक (*pāka*) in the second meaning means one of unripe mind has been told in the explanation of the sentence पाकः पृच्छामि मनसा विजानन् (*pākaḥ pṛcchāmi manasā vijānan*) in the 5th Ṛk of this same sūkta. The author of the Nirukta, too, explaining this, says पाकः पक्तव्यो भवति विपक्षप्रज्ञ आत्मेत्यात्मगतिमाचष्टे (*pākaḥ paktavyo bhavati vipakṣaprajña ātmetyātmagatimācaṣṭe*).
*[as supplied: the garbled label "ವ್ಯಾಕರಣ, ಕ್ರಿಯಾ" stands before the grammar section; the script normalised it.]*

*Grammar (transcribed, not explained):*
यत्र (*yatra*)—निपातस्यच (*nipātasyaca*) (Pā. Sū. 6-3-136), lengthening in the saṃhitā. अमृतस्य (*amṛtasya*)—नञो जरमर (*naño jaramara*) (Pā. Sū. 6-2-116), the final member has initial udātta. अनिमेषम् (*animeṣam*)—तत्पुरुषे तुल्यार्थ (*tatpuruṣe tulyārtha*) (Pā. Sū. 6-2-2), the original accent of the first member.
विदथा (*vidathā*)—root विदज्ञाने (*vidajñāne*) (printed joined); रुदिविदिभ्यांजुत् (*rudividibhyāṃjut*) (Uṇ. Sū. 3-395), ending atha; as jit-ness is laid down, no guṇa for the penultimate of the root; initial udātta from the ending; before the instrumental case-ending, सुपां सुलुक् (*supāṃ suluk*) gives the lengthening to the preceding homogeneous vowel.
अभिस्वरंति (*abhisvaraṃti*)—root स्व गत् (*sva gat*) *[as supplied: so printed]*, bhvādi; laṭ third person plural, ending jha; झोंतः (*jhoṃtaḥ*) for the substitute anta; śap-vikaraṇa; सार्वधातुकार्धधातुकयोः (*sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*) for

guṇa of the ṛ-vowel, with r following; no nighāta accent because of the connection with यत्र (*yatra*); by the sūtra तास्यनुदात्तेत् (*tāsyanudāttet*) the lasārvadhātuka is unaccented, so the root-accent remains; by तिजुचोदात्तवति (*tijucodāttavati*) (Pā. #### Ṛk 22
**॥ संहितापाठः ॥**
> यस्मि॑न्वृ॒क्षे म॒ध्वदः॑ सुप॒र्णा नि॑वि॒शंते॒ सुव॑ते॒ चाधि॒ विश्वे॑ ।
> तस्यॆदा॑हुः॒ पिप्स॑लं स्वा॒द्वग्रे॒ तन्नोन्न॑श॒द्यः पि॒तरं॒ न वेद॑ ॥२२॥
*[as supplied: the garbled label "ಪವನಾಡಿ" stands after the Saṃhitā block, normalised by the script to Pada-pāṭha.]*
**॥ पदपाठः ॥**
> यस्मिन् । वृक्षे ! मधुअदः । सुपर्णाः । निविशंते । सुवते । च । अधि । विश्वे !
> तस्य । इत् । आहुः । पिप्पलं । स्वादु । अग्रे । तत् । न । उत् । नशत् । यः । पितरं ।
> न । वेद ॥ २२ ॥
**॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥**
> अत्र वृक्षस्वरूपकल्पना । अधिदैवमादित्यमध्यात्ममात्मानं च प्रशंसति । यस्मिन्नादित्ये वृक्षे वृक्षवत्सर्वफलाश्रयभूते मध्वदः । मध्वित्युदकनाम । तददंतीति
> मध्वद उदकस्यात्तारः सुपर्णाः सुपतना रश्मयो निविशंते प्रविशंति रात्र्य सुवते च
> पुनरुदयकाले प्रकाशं जनयंति च यस्मादादित्यात् । कुत्र । आधि विश्वे विश्वस्योपरि।

*Gist:* In the sun as tree the rays enter at night and spread light at dawn; read spiritually, the senses sink into the Self; its fruit is gained only by one who knows the protector.

**प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)**
यस्मिन् (*yasmin*)—in which, in the form of the sun; वृक्षे (*vṛkṣe*)—in the tree; मध्यदः (*madhyadaḥ*) *[as supplied: the Ṛk has मध्वदः (*madhvadaḥ*)]*—those that feed on water; सुपर्णाः (*suparṇāḥ*)—rays; निविशंते (*niviśaṃte*)—enter (at night-time, and again at the time of rising); अधि विश्वे (*adhi viśve*)—over all the worlds; सुवते च (*suvate ca*)—spread (the sun's) light; तस्य इत् (*tasya it*)—of that same sun; पिप्पलं (*pippalaṃ*)—the fruit that protects; स्वादु (*svādu*)—as full of savour; अग्रे (*agre*)—as the best (above all other fruits); आहुः (*āhuḥ*)—the knowers of truth say; यः (*yaḥ*)—which man; पितरं (*pitaraṃ*)—the sun, protector of the world; न वेद (*na veda*)—does not know (through worship and the like); तत् (*tat*)—that fruit; न उन्नशत् (*na unnaśat*)—does not obtain *[as supplied: the dash after न उन्नशत् (*na unnaśat*) is lacking in the print]*.

**भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)**
In which tree, in the form of the sun, the rays that feed on water enter at night-time, and again at the time of rising spread the sun's light over all the worlds, of that same sun the fruit that protects the knowers of truth call full of savour and the best of all other fruits. The man who does not know, through worship and the like, the sun, protector of the world, does not obtain that fruit.

**Printed English**

### Printed p. 427
*Running head: ಅ. ೨. ಅ. ೩. ವ. ೧೫. ] ಋಗ್ವೇದಸಂಹಿತಾ 427 (as supplied).*

fruit sweet, but he partakes not of it who knows not the protector (of the universe).

**विशेषविषयगळु (Viśeṣaviṣayagaḷu)**
Here, on the side relating to the divinity, the sun is praised, and on the spiritual side the Self. It is said that those who worship, by worship and the like, that sun in whom the rays enter at night and again at the time of rising spread his light to the world, enjoy the fruit that is in the tree in the form of the sun, extremely sweet and the best of all other fruits, and that for the rest it is not attainable. By पितरः न वेद (*pitaraḥ na veda*) ("who does not know the protector") the primacy is given to knowledge. It is stated that for tasting that fruit the knowledge of the nature of the sun is absolutely necessary. This is on the side relating to the divinity. On the spiritual side:
यस्मिन्परमात्मनि वृक्षे सुपर्णाः शोभनगमनानींद्रियाणि मध्वदः ज्ञानस्यात्त्वाणि निविशंते स्वापकाले स्वस्वविषयेभ्यः प्रतिनिवृत्तानि पुनः प्रबोधकाले विश्वस्योपरि सुवते स्वस्वविषयान् लभंते । तस्य परमात्मनः पिप्वलं पालकं .... .... .... .... ॥ (*yasminparamātmani vṛkṣe suparṇāḥ śobhanagamanānīṃdriyāṇi madhvadaḥ jñānasyāttvāṇi niviśaṃte svāpakāle svasvaviṣayebhyaḥ pratinivṛttāni punaḥ prabodhakāle viśvasyopari suvate svasvaviṣayān labhaṃte | tasya paramātmanaḥ pipvalaṃ pālakaṃ .... .... .... .... ‖*) *[as supplied: पिप्वलं (*pipvalaṃ*) for पिप्पलं (*pippalaṃ*); ellipses as printed.]*
In which tree in the form of the Supreme Self the senses, easy movers, that experience the savour of knowledge, at the time of sleep turn back from their objects and are absorbed in the Self alone, and afterwards at the time of waking again come into contact with their objects, the nature of that Supreme Self, to be gained by experiencing it, is extremely sweet and the best of all other fruits. But if it is asked for whom the enjoyment of this fruit is possible, or for whom it is not to be gained, then यः पितरं न वेद न तन्नोन्नशत् (*yaḥ pitaraṃ na veda na tannonnaśat*) means: it is gained by one who knows the nature of this Supreme Self, the protector; it is not gained by the ignorant who does not know. In this manner, passages are many, in the Saṃhitā and in the Āraṇyakas and elsewhere, that state the identity of the sun and the Supreme Self and have a description and praise of one form. For example,
मरीचयः स्वायंभुवाः । ये शरीराण्यकल्पयन् । ते ते देहं कल्पयंतु मा च ते ख्यास्मै तीरिषत् । उत्तिष्ठत मा स्वप्त । अग्निमिच्छध्वं भारताः । राज्ञः सोमस्य तृप्नसः । सूर्येण सयुजोषसः । युवा सुवासाः । अष्टाचक्रा नवद्वारा । देवानां पूरयोध्या । तस्याग्ं हिरण्मयः कोशः । स्वर्गो लोको ज्योतिषावृतः । यो वै तां ब्रह्मणो वेद । अमृतेनावृतां पुरीं ! तस्मै ब्रह्म च ब्रह्माच । आयुः कीर्तिं प्रजां ददुः । विभ्राजमानाग्ं हरिणीं। यशसा संपरीवृतां । पुरग्ं हिरण्मयिं ब्रह्मा ॥ (*marīcayaḥ svāyaṃbhuvāḥ | ye śarīrāṇyakalpayan | te te dehaṃ kalpayaṃtu mā ca te khyāsmai tīriṣat | uttiṣṭhata mā svapta | agnimicchadhvaṃ bhāratāḥ | rājñaḥ somasya tṛpnasaḥ | sūryeṇa sayujoṣasaḥ | yuvā suvāsāḥ | aṣṭācakrā navadvārā | devānāṃ pūrayodhyā | tasyāgṃ hiraṇmayaḥ kośaḥ | svargo loko jyotiṣāvṛtaḥ | yo vai tāṃ brahmaṇo veda | amṛtenāvṛtāṃ purīṃ ! tasmai brahma ca brahmāca | āyuḥ kīrtiṃ prajāṃ daduḥ | vibhrājamānāgṃ hariṇīṃ| yaśasā saṃparīvṛtāṃ | puragṃ hiraṇmayiṃ brahmā ‖*)
(Śrī. Ā. 1-27-2, 3) *[as supplied: so printed.]*

### Printed p. 428
*Running head: 438 ಸಾಯಣಭಾಷ್ಯಸಹಿತಾ [ ಮಂ ೭. ಅ. ೨೨ ಸೂ ೧೬.] (as supplied; the page is 428, and "438", "ಮಂ ೭" and "ಸೂ ೧೬" are printed so).*

In these sentences all the elements that are in the Ṛk at hand are found. Here the sense conveyed by the word सुपर्ण (*suparṇa*) is indicated by the word मरीचयः (*marīcayaḥ*). रश्मयः शरीरान्यात्मोपासकदेहानकल्पयन्कृतवंतस्ते तव देहं कल्पयंतु । (*raśmayaḥ śarīrānyātmopāsakadehānakalpayankṛtavaṃtaste tava dehaṃ kalpayaṃtu |*) It is understood as the rays, members of the body of the sun, and as the senses and other members of the body that serve as the means of worshipping the Self. Such rays, or such senses and other members, join the Supreme Self in the form of the sun, and again prepare the way for the welfare of the world and the welfare of the self. But for these to become instruments of welfare, the knowledge of the nature of the sun, or of the Supreme Self in the form of the sun, must above all be indispensable. This chief point is stated in the Ṛk at hand in a prohibitive form as यः पितरं न वेद नोन्नशत् (*yaḥ pitaraṃ na veda nonnaśat*), and in the Āraṇyaka sentence in an injunctive form as यो वै तां ब्रह्मणो वेद (*yo vai tāṃ brahmaṇo veda*). The words पिप्पलं फलं स्वादु (*pippalaṃ phalaṃ svādu*) are explained by the sentence अमृतेनावृतां पुरीं (*amṛtenāvṛtāṃ purīṃ*). No other fruit can give the satisfaction that is gained from this state, which is of the nature of supreme bliss. If the question arises, "Are there not other fruits, in the form of heaven and the like?", Sāyaṇa answers it with इतरस्वर्गादिफलानि पुनर्जननाद्यापादकत्वात् आपातस्वादूनि । (*itarasvargādiphalāni punarjananādyāpādakatvāt āpātasvādūni |*): since the other fruits, heaven and the rest, cause birth again and again, they are not fruits as good as this bliss in the form of immortality; this he has made clear. Before understanding the descriptions in the Upaniṣads and elsewhere that likewise show the identity of the sun and the Supreme Self, one must examine the proper meaning of the sentences in the Ṛk at hand that explain the description of the sun, who is the divinity, the nature of the rays that are his members, on the spiritual side the description of the Self, and the nature of the senses and the rest, members of the body that is its support, and how the senses, attached to their objects, enter the Self and become instruments of the bliss of the Self.
On the side relating to the divinity: for the word वृक्षे (*vṛkṣe*) the explanation वृक्षवत् सर्वफलाश्रयभूते (*vṛkṣavat sarvaphalāśrayabhūte*) is given: "in the one who, like a tree, is the support of all kinds of fruit" (in the sun). Or it would not be wrong to explain also that, as a tree is the support of all kinds of beings, the sun is the support of all worlds.
धर्ता दिवो विभाति तपसस्पृथिव्यामिति । धर्ता ह्येष दिवो विभाति तपस स्पृथिव्यां धर्ता देवो वेदानाममर्त्यस्तपोज्जा ॥ (*dhartā divo vibhāti tapasaspṛthivyāmiti | dhartā hyeṣa divo vibhāti tapasa spṛthivyāṃ dhartā devo vedānāmamartyastapojjā ‖*)
(Ca. Prā. 14-1-9) *[as supplied: the reference is printed "ಚ. ಪ್ರಾ. ೧೪-೧-೯-:-"; kept as printed.]*
In such sentences both these meanings are indicated, and since the sun is described as the supporter of all worlds and the giver of the fruits of all worlds, the sun is the support of all and the giver of all fruits.

### Printed p. 429
*Running head: ಅ. ೨. ಅ. ೩. ವ. ೧೮. । ಋಗ್ವೇದಸಂಹಿತಾ 429 (as supplied).*

*[Continuing the Special Topics of Ṛk 22 from the previous window; this window contains no Sanskrit block.]*
It was explained earlier that the word सुपर्ण (*suparṇa*) means a ray, and that these same rays, drawing water from the earth and gathering it in the sun, become the cause of the fall of rain. It is because they take in the juice in the form of water that these rays have the qualifier मध्वरः (*madhvaraḥ*) *[as supplied: differs from the word in the Ṛk]*. मद्वित्युदकनाम । तत् अदंतीति मध्वरः उदकस्य अत्तारः । (*madvityudakanāma | tat adaṃtīti madhvaraḥ udakasya attāraḥ |*) *[as supplied: "ಮದ್ವಿ-" for the expected "ಮಧ್ವಿ-"]* Madhu means water. Sāyaṇa has explained that, because they feed on it, the qualifier मध्वरः (*madhvaraḥ*) is given to the rays. These rays, lying asleep in the sun at night-time, appear outside at the time of rising and spread the sun's light over the whole world.
Describing the fruit of this tree in the form of the sun, पिप्पलं स्वादु (*pippalaṃ svādu*) is told to be a fruit that protects and is full of savour. And by the word अग्रे (*agre*) it is indicated that it is better than all other fruits. The variety and the greatness of this fruit, to be brought by the sun, are described and praised in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka as follows. Here, showing the identity of the Supreme Self who dwells in the heart with the sun, it is told that the gods also sought out this sun and obtained the fruit to be had from him. Besides, stating the relation between action and knowledge, it praises both as giving one and the same fruit.
परेण तंतुं परिषिच्यमानं । अंतरादित्ये मनसा चरंतं । देवानाग्ं हृदयं ब्रह्मान्वविंदत् । ब्रह्मैतद्ब्रह्मण उज्जभार। अर्कग् श्चोतंतग्ं सरिरस्य मध्ये । आ यस्मिन्त्सप्तपेरवः । मेहंति बहुलाग् श्रियं । बह्वश्वामिंद्र गोमतीं ॥ (*pareṇa taṃtuṃ pariṣicyamānaṃ | aṃtarāditye manasā caraṃtaṃ | devānāgṃ hṛdayaṃ brahmānvaviṃdat | brahmaitadbrahmaṇa ujjabhāra| arkag ścotaṃtagṃ sarirasya madhye | ā yasmintsaptaperavaḥ | mehaṃti bahulāg śriyaṃ | bahvaśvāmiṃdra gomatīṃ ‖*)
(Tai. Ā. 3-11-6)
Prajāpati sought out the Supreme Self who is in the heart of Indra and the other gods, and at last obtained sight of him. This Supreme Self moves in the orb of the sun in order to pour rain at the time when he gives the fruit to sacrifices, rites of yajña and the like. Entering, in the form of the sun's rays, the midst of the water that stands in the clouds, this Supreme Self pours down the fruit in the form of rain. In this sun the seven rays, protectors of the world, have gathered and obtained shelter. (This is described in Ṛks such as साकंजानां सप्तथमाहु रेकजं (*sākaṃjānāṃ saptathamāhu rekajaṃ*).) These rays, pouring down the rain that is the cause of the wealth of plants and the rest, protect the world. They supply riches such as cattle.
अच्युतां बहुलाग् श्रियं । स हरिर्वसुवित्तमः । सेरुरिंद्राय पिन्वते । .... .... .... .... शतग्ं शता अस्य युक्ता हरीणां । अर्वाजायातु वसुभी रश्मिरिंद्रः .... .... .... .... .... .... । (*acyutāṃ bahulāg śriyaṃ | sa harirvasuvittamaḥ | seruriṃdrāya pinvate | .... .... .... .... śatagṃ śatā asya yuktā harīṇāṃ | arvājāyātu vasubhī raśmiriṃdraḥ .... .... .... .... .... .... |*) *[ellipses as printed.]*
(Tai. Ā. 3-11-7)

### Printed p. 430
*Running head: 430 ಸಾಯಣಭಾಷ್ಯಸಹಿತಾ [ ಮಂ. ೧. ಆ. ೨೨. ಸೂ. ೧೬೪] (as supplied).*

भद्रं पश्यंत उपसेदुरग्रे । तपो दीक्षामृषयः सुवर्विदः । ततः क्षत्रं बलमोजश्च जातं । तदस्मै देवा अभि सन्नमंतु । श्वेतग्ं रश्मिं बोभुज्यमानं । अपां नेतारं भुवनस्य गोपां ॥ (*bhadraṃ paśyaṃta upaseduragre | tapo dīkṣāmṛṣayaḥ suvarvidaḥ | tataḥ kṣatraṃ balamojaśca jātaṃ | tadasmai devā abhi sannamaṃtu | śvetagṃ raśmiṃ bobhujyamānaṃ | apāṃ netāraṃ bhuvanasya gopāṃ ‖*)
(Tai. Ā. 3-11-9)
These rays of the sun distribute among the world the fruits to be gained from the sun. What are they? The imperishable and abundant riches of cattle and the like. The sages who travel the road to heaven, desiring to gain these riches, approached the sun, who is in the form of the seven hotṛs, and by worshipping him with upāsana and the like, by his grace obtained strength of the kṣatra kind and vigour; may the sacrificers too obtain the same riches. That is, by worship of the sun all these are gained. Among these, one kind is the mass of riches such as food that nourishes the world; the other kind is the kṣatra riches able to protect it. There is nothing sweeter than these riches that are gained from the sun. These are riches that guard the world. Explaining what these rays of the sun are like and what their actions are:
रोहिणीः पिंगळा एकरूपाः । क्षरंतीः पिंगळा एकरूपाः । शतग्ं सहस्राणि प्रयुतानि नाव्यानां । (*rohiṇīḥ piṃgaḷā ekarūpāḥ | kṣaraṃtīḥ piṃgaḷā ekarūpāḥ | śatagṃ sahasrāṇi prayutāni nāvyānāṃ |*)
(Tri. Ā. 3-18-19) *[as supplied: so printed, "ತ್ರಿ. ಆ."]*
The waters that flow over the regions of the earth, both of red hue and of tawny hue, drawn by the rays and standing in the clouds, give up their various forms and acquire oneness of form. Then again they flow over the earth in streams, in hundreds and in thousands. All this is the grace of the sun in the form of the seven hotṛs. The knowledge of such a sun is absolutely necessary. By his worship alone all wealth is gained. " तन्नोन्नशद्यः पितरं न वेद (*tannonnaśadyaḥ pitaraṃ na veda*) ". Since his grace is not possible unless one knows the nature of such a sun and the manner of his worship and worships him with the prescribed rites, the poets seek him out. This manner of seeking is described in the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā itself in the following way. Although in this description there is the manner of meditative seeking described in the Upaniṣad, knowledge seems to be a means both to action and to obtaining its fruit. For example—
पतंगमक्तमसुरस्य मायया हृदा पश्यंति मनसा मनीषिणः । समुद्रे अंतः कवयो वि चक्षते मरीचीनां पदमिच्छंति वेधसः ॥ पतंगो वाचं मनसा बिभर्ति तां गंधर्वोऽवदद्गर्भे अंत । तां द्योतमानां स्वर्यं मनीषामृतस्य पदे कवयो निशांति । (*pataṃgamaktamasurasya māyayā hṛdā paśyaṃti manasā manīṣiṇaḥ | samudre aṃtaḥ kavayo vi cakṣate marīcīnāṃ padamicchaṃti vedhasaḥ ‖ pataṃgo vācaṃ manasā bibharti tāṃ gaṃdharvo 'vadadgarbhe aṃta | tāṃ dyotamānāṃ svaryaṃ manīṣāmṛtasya pade kavayo niśāṃti |*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-12-1, -1) *[as supplied: so printed, the second figure repeated as "-೧".]*

### Printed p. 431
*Running head: ಅ ೨. ಅ. ೩. ವ. ೧೮. ] ಋಗ್ವೇದಸಂಹಿತಾ 431 (as supplied).*

Great sages who know the Veda and the śāstras meditate on and realise the sun, who is pervaded by the inconceivable power of the Supreme Self, with their inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is in the heart-lotus and is controlled. They praise specially this sun who shines in the midst of the atmosphere, like the sea. Skilful performers, the sacrificers, carry out their rites and the like in order to obtain union (sāyujya) with the sun, the support of the rays. This sun impels creatures to utter the shining words of the Veda and the like. The knowers of the śāstras recite the Vedic sentences that concern the Supreme Brahman and thereby again satisfy the Supreme Self. All this is the greatness of the sun. In such descriptions identity is stated between the Supreme Self, who is formless and without change, and the sun, who is visible to ordinary perception. Not only this: not aiming only at spiritual riches, worldly happiness and the like are also desired.
पंचारं चक्रं परिवर्तते पृथु । हिरण्यज्योतिः सरिरस्य मध्यॆ । अजस्रं ज्योतिर्नभसा सर्पदेति । स न इंद्रः कामवरं ददातु । (*paṃcāraṃ cakraṃ parivartate pṛthu | hiraṇyajyotiḥ sarirasya madhyè | ajasraṃ jyotirnabhasā sarpadeti | sa na iṃdraḥ kāmavaraṃ dadātu |*)
(Śrī. Ā. 3-11-8) *[as supplied: so printed, "ಶ್ರೀ. ಆ."]*
In this and similar texts, as described before, the sun, who has five spokes in the form of the seasons, who is in the form of the wheel of time, and who is united with the Supreme Lord, is prayed to: "may he bring all our desires to fulfilment." In this way, desiring the fruit of action, worshipping the Supreme Self who stands in the middle of the sun, visible to ordinary perception, looking for the fruits to be gained with the help of his rays, and praising the sun as protector of the world (as father): this became the meaning on the side relating to the divinity.
The meaning of the spiritual side, which is not manifest, has been briefly told above. That the two forms of the Supreme Brahman, the manifest and the unmanifest, are both contained within the orb of the sun is described in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka as follows.
द्वे वाव ब्रह्मणो रूपे मूर्तं चैवामूर्तं च मर्त्यं चामृतं च स्थितं च यच्च सच्च त्यच्च । (*dve vāva brahmaṇo rūpe mūrtaṃ caivāmūrtaṃ ca martyaṃ cāmṛtaṃ ca sthitaṃ ca yacca sacca tyacca |*)
(Bṛ. U. 2-3-1)
The form of the Supreme Brahman is twofold: that which has form and that which has none; the mortal and the immortal; the stable and the moving; that with particular marks and that without them.
तदेतन्नूर्तं यदन्यद्वायोश्चांतरिक्षाच्चैतन्मर्त्यमेतत्स्थितमेतत्सत्तस्य मूर्तस्यैतस्य मर्त्यस्यैतस्य स्थितस्यैतस्य सत विष रसो य विष तपति सतो ह्येष रसः ॥ (*tadetannūrtaṃ yadanyadvāyoścāṃtarikṣāccaitanmartyametatsthitametatsattasya mūrtasyaitasya martyasyaitasya sthitasyaitasya sata viṣa raso ya viṣa tapati sato hyeṣa rasaḥ ‖*) *[as supplied: the print has "ನೂರ್ತಂ" and "ವಿಷ" for the expected forms; kept as printed.]*
(Bṛ. U. 2-3-2) *[as supplied: reference printed "ಬೃ. ತಾ. ೨-೩-೨"]*

### Printed p. 432
*Running head: 432 ಸಾಯಣಭಾಷ್ಯಸಹಿತಾ [ಮಂ. ೧. ಅ. ೨೨. ಸೂ. ೧೬೪] (as supplied).*

Everything that is other than the air and the atmosphere is mortal, stable and with particular marks. The essence of all things that are of the nature of the elements, mortal, stable and of the nature of being, is this shining sun. The essence of the form that has shape and is of the nature of existence is the sun. This is one of the two forms of the Supreme Brahman. Besides,
अथामूर्तं वायुश्चांतरिक्षं चैतदमृतमेतद्यदेतत्त्यत्तस्यैतस्यामूर्तस्यैतस्यामृतस्यैतस्य यत एतस्य त्यस्यैष रसो य एष एतस्मिन्मंडले पुरुषस्तस्य ह्येष रस इत्यधिदैवतं ॥ (*athāmūrtaṃ vāyuścāṃtarikṣaṃ caitadamṛtametadyadetattyattasyaitasyāmūrtasyaitasyāmṛtasyaitasya yata etasya tyasyaiṣa raso ya eṣa etasminmaṃḍale puruṣastasya hyeṣa rasa ityadhidaivataṃ ‖*)
(Bṛ. U. 2 3-3) *[as supplied: so printed, without the hyphen after "2".]*
What is without shape is the air and the atmosphere; they are immortal and without particular marks. The essence of these also is this shining sun. The essence of the things without particular marks is also this same sun. This is the adhidaivata. Thus a twofold description is shown on the side relating to the divinity also, showing that the sun is the support of both these forms of the Supreme Brahman; then, telling the spiritual form of the Supreme Brahman, it is described in the Upaniṣads and elsewhere that even the Supreme Self, who can be realised by meditation in the form of samādhi alone, is a dweller in the middle of the orb of the sun. For example—
आदित्यो ना ब्रह्मेत्यादेशः । स य एतमेवं विद्वानादित्यं ब्रह्मेत्युपास्ते ॥ (*ādityo nā brahmetyādeśaḥ | sa ya etamevaṃ vidvānādityaṃ brahmetyupāste ‖*)
(Bhā. U. 3-19-1 and 4) *[as supplied: reference printed "ಭಾ. ಉ. ೩-೧೯-೧ ಮತ್ತು ೪"; "ನಾ" is printed in the quotation.]*
In sentences of this kind the sun is praised as Brahman, and it is told that the sun is to be worshipped as Brahman. In the explanation of the spiritual side of the Ṛk at hand, the description of the nature of this all-pervading Supreme Self, the description of the nature of the fruit gained by realising that Supreme Self, and the need of knowledge of the Lord, the means to experience this fruit, are stated in order.
Here the Supreme Self is likened to a tree. Sāyaṇa has explained वृक्षवत् गमनादिरहिते अविक्रिये (*vṛkṣavat gamanādirahite avikriye*) as: the highest principle that, like a tree, is motionless and unchanging. The same description is found also in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, in this way.
यस्मात्परं नापरमस्ति किंचिद्यस्मान्नाणीयो न ज्यायोऽस्ति कश्चित् । वृक्ष इव स्तब्धो दिवि तिष्ठत्येकस्तेनेदं पूर्णं पुरुषेण सर्वं ॥ (*yasmātparaṃ nāparamasti kiṃcidyasmānnāṇīyo na jyāyo 'sti kaścit | vṛkṣa iva stabdho divi tiṣṭhatyekastenedaṃ pūrṇaṃ puruṣeṇa sarvaṃ ‖*)
(Śrī. 88 4-10) *[as supplied: so printed.]*
The one Supreme Self, without a second, stands like a tree, free from coming and going, still and unchanging, and is himself the self of the whole universe. Since this Brahman-principle is without a second, there is nothing higher or lower than it. But what is the place of this Supreme Self?

### Printed p. 433
*Running head: ಅ. ೨. ಅ. ೩. ವ. ೧೮. ] ಋಗ್ವೇದಸಂಹಿತಾ 433 (as supplied).*

परेण नाकं निहितं गुहायां विभ्राजते यद्यतयो विशंति ॥ (*pareṇa nākaṃ nihitaṃ guhāyāṃ vibhrājate yadyatayo viśaṃti ‖*)
(Śrī. A. 10-10-5) *[as supplied: so printed, "ಶ್ರೀ. ಅ."]*
Ascetics who are of self-controlling mind cause it to shine in their own intellect, which is higher than heaven, one-pointed, in the form of a cave, and themselves enter into it and are absorbed in it. How that is can be seen in the description of the Ṛk at hand.
यस्मिन्परमात्मनि सुपर्णाः शोभनगमनानींद्रियाणि मध्वदो मधुनो ज्ञानस्यात्त्वणि तज्ञा नेन ज्ञानभांजीत्यर्थः । (*yasminparamātmani suparṇāḥ śobhanagamanānīṃdriyāṇi madhvado madhuno jñānasyāttvaṇi tajñā nena jñānabhāṃjītyarthaḥ |*) *[as supplied: "ತಜ್ಞಾ ನೇನ" is split by a line-break.]*
The qualifier सुपर्णाः (*suparṇāḥ*) is stated in order to show a characteristic fitting the nature of those senses, with good movements, which enter the Supreme Self and there take their share in the realisation of the knowledge of the Self. But निविशंते (*niviśaṃte*); अधि विश्वे सुवते च (*adhi viśve suvate ca*): entering within and again appearing outside: from this, what is the duty of the senses? To tell what relation there is between the senses, with such comings and goings, and the Self, Sāyaṇa has explained as follows.
निविशंते स्वापकाले स्वस्वविषयेभ्यः प्रतिनिवृत्तानि आत्मनिवृत्ता लीयंते पुनः प्रबोधकाले अधि विश्वे विश्वस्कोपरि सुवते च उद्यंति । स्वस्वविषयान् लभंते इत्यर्थः । (*niviśaṃte svāpakāle svasvaviṣayebhyaḥ pratinivṛttāni ātmanivṛttā līyaṃte punaḥ prabodhakāle adhi viśve viśvaskopari suvate ca udyaṃti | svasvaviṣayān labhaṃte ityarthaḥ |*)
At the time of sleep (the time of deep sleep) the senses leave their objects, withdraw from contact with objects and are absorbed in the Self. Then at the time of waking they appear again facing the universe and come into contact with their own objects. This is the description of the functions of the senses. What is the relation of these functions of the senses to the Supreme Self? In which state of these functions of the senses does realisation of the Self take place? What is the nature of the fruit gained by that realisation? What is its distinction? This is told in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad in this way. First,
" परांचि खानि व्यतृणत्स्वयंभूस्तस्मात् पराज् पश्यति नांतरात्मन् ॥ (*parāṃci khāni vyatṛṇatsvayaṃbhūstasmāt parāj paśyati nāṃtarātman ‖*)
*[as supplied: the reference is printed twice, garbled: "(ಕಠ. ಉ. ೨" and then "(ಕರ. ಉ. ೨-೧-೧)"; read as Kaṭha. U. 2-1-1, kept as printed.]*
The hearing and other senses are left to be always attached to outer objects; when there is the connection of the senses, which find satisfaction in outer objects alone and are smeared with desire and the like, the Self has the waking state. Then all the activities of the suparṇas, that is, of the senses, are only outward. This state is described in the Māṇḍūkya as the first quarter of the Self. How is that?
*[as supplied: at the foot of the page the signature marks "[28] [Vol. 12" are printed twice, the second time in spaced form; they stay here as stray lines.]*

### Printed p. 434
*Running head: 434 ಸಾಯಣಭಾಷ್ಯಸಹಿತಾ [ ಮಂ. ೧ ಅ. ೨೨. ಸೂ ೧೬೪] (as supplied).*

जागरितस्थानो बहिष्पृज्ञः सप्तांग एकोनविंशतिमुखः स्कूलभुग्वैश्वानरः प्रथमः पादः ॥ (*jāgaritasthāno bahiṣpṛjñaḥ saptāṃga ekonaviṃśatimukhaḥ skūlabhugvaiśvānaraḥ prathamaḥ pādaḥ ‖*)
(Mā. U. 1-3)
Since waking is the place of the Self, in this state he is called "having waking as his place". Because his knowledge is directed outside, that is, to objects other than himself, he is "outward-knowing" बहिष्पृज्ञः (*bahiṣpṛjñaḥ*) *[as supplied: so printed]*. He has seven limbs and nineteen mouths (5 organs of knowledge, 5 organs of action, 5 airs, mind, intellect, ego and thought). Through these doors the Self, whose view is outward, goes on enjoying gross objects such as sound. This is the first quarter, or state, of the Self.
स्वप्नःस्थानोऽंतःप्रज्ञः सप्तांग एकोनविंशतिमुखः प्रविविक्तमुखः तैजसो द्वितीयः पादः ॥ (*svapnaḥsthāno 'ṃtaḥprajñaḥ saptāṃga ekonaviṃśatimukhaḥ praviviktamukhaḥ taijaso dvitīyaḥ pādaḥ ‖*)
(Mā. U. 1-4)
The Self in this state is named Taijasa. He is "having dream as his place". The awareness of waking comes about through many means such as the eye and the other senses and seems to have objects outside; it is only a movement of the mind and produces just such an impression in the mind. That mind, thus impressed, like a cloth with a picture painted on it, without desiring an outside means, driven by ignorance, desire and action, appears just like waking. Therefore:
अस्य लोकस्य सर्वावतो मात्रामपादाय । (*asya lokasya sarvāvato mātrāmapādāya |*)
(Bṛ. U. 4-3-9)
Taking the impression of waking, with all its means and riches, he experiences the dream. Because the mind alone is inside the senses, and for the reason that the awareness of it in the form of impressions takes place for him in the dream, he is called, in this state, "inward-knowing". Yet here the awareness that is in the form of impressions is what is enjoyed. This is the second quarter. Besides,
यत्र सुप्तो न कंचन कामं कामयते न कंचन स्वप्नं पश्यति तत् सुषुप्तं । सुषुप्तस्थान एकीभूत प्रज्ञानघन एवानंदमयो ह्यानंदभुक्चेतो मुखः प्राज्ञस्मृतीयः पादः ॥ (*yatra supto na kaṃcana kāmaṃ kāmayate na kaṃcana svapnaṃ paśyati tat suṣuptaṃ | suṣuptasthāna ekībhūta prajñānaghana evānaṃdamayo hyānaṃdabhukceto mukhaḥ prājñasmṛtīyaḥ pādaḥ ‖*) *[as supplied: "ಪ್ರಾಜ್ಞಸ್ಮೃತೀಯಃ" for the expected "ಪ್ರಾಜ್ಞಸ್ತೃತೀಯಃ"; kept as printed.]*
(Mā. U. 1-5)
In this state the Self is asleep. He desires no desire. He sees no dream. At this time he is "having deep sleep as his place" *[as supplied: "ಸುಮಪ್ತಸ್ಥಾನ" is printed for "ಸುಷುಪ್ತಸ್ಥಾನ"]*, become one, a mass of knowledge, full of bliss, an enjoyer of bliss, having thought as his mouth. This is the third quarter. And the mind, objects *[as supplied: the text breaks off at the end of the page at "ಮನಸ್ಸು ವಿಷಯ" and continues in the next window.]*
